Each structure is typically represented as a smooth tube or "worm" tracing the path of the protein backbone. This method provides a clear visual impression of the conformational variability and dynamic fluctuations within the molecular ensemble. (UNVERIFIED)

A helical density map is a visualization method used to represent the three-dimensional distribution of atoms within a helical structure, averaged over time from a simulation. It creates a 3D grid where the value at each point represents the probability of finding an atom, which can then be displayed as a contoured surface. This method is particularly useful for analyzing the average structure and packing of molecules like DNA or alpha-helical proteins. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational method for placing ions, like sodium or chloride, into a simulation box containing a charged molecule like a protein. It works by calculating the electrostatic potential around the molecule and then using a mathematical operator, the Laplacian, to identify the most electrostatically favorable positions for the ions to be placed. This approach is more physically realistic than simply placing ions randomly, as it positions them in regions where they are most likely to be found, such as near oppositely charged amino acid residues.

An enhanced sampling simulation technique that enhances traditional biased molecular dynamics to calculate binding affinities, mechanical unfolding pathways, and free energy profiles (e.g., Potential of Mean Force) in biomolecules. It applies an evolving, position-dependent energy bias to help the system escape local minima along a specific reaction coordinate.

Driven adaptively biased molecular dynamics (d-ABMD) is an enhanced sampling technique that combines two approaches to explore a specific molecular process. It uses an adaptive biasing potential, like in metadynamics, to overcome energy barriers, while simultaneously applying an external "driving" force to guide the system along a predefined reaction coordinate. This dual approach is particularly effective for efficiently calculating the free energy profile of a complex conformational change that is too slow to occur spontaneously.

Redox potential replica-exchange molecular dynamics is a specialized version of the REMD method where the different parallel simulations are run at different electrochemical redox potentials, rather than different temperatures. This allows the system to efficiently sample different oxidation states in a simulation that is coupled to an electron bath.

A restrained simulation is a type of simulation where an additional, artificial energy potential is applied to guide the system's motion. These restraints can be used to force a molecule to adopt a certain conformation, to prevent it from moving too far, or to incorporate experimental data into the simulation. Restraints are a powerful tool for targeted sampling, structure refinement, and calculating potentials of mean force.

An electron microscopy map restraint method is a simulation technique where the simulation is guided by a three-dimensional density map obtained from an electron microscopy experiment. An additional energy term is added that penalizes conformations where the simulated atoms do not fit well into the experimental density. For structural biologists, this method is a powerful tool for refining low-resolution experimental structures into high-resolution, physically realistic atomic models.

A numerical method that solves a differential equation by replacing each derivative with the difference between values at nearby grid points. The continuous problem becomes a large set of simultaneous equations, one per grid point. It is how the Poisson-Boltzmann equation is solved for a molecular shape. (UNVERIFIED)

A branch of mathematics concerned with computing approximate answers to problems that cannot be solved exactly. Almost every step of a simulation rests on it, because the equations of motion and the integrals of statistical mechanics have no closed-form solutions for a real molecule. Its central concern is how large the approximation error is and whether it accumulates. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical method for solving a differential equation across a boundary where the solution or its derivative jumps, such as the surface between a solute and continuum solvent. It modifies the finite-difference stencil near the boundary to take the known jump conditions into account, instead of smoothing over them. In this field it is used to solve the Poisson-Boltzmann equation accurately at the molecular surface. (UNVERIFIED)

An enhanced sampling method that generates new conformations by displacing a structure along its slowest collective modes rather than at random. Those modes are the directions in which the molecule moves most easily, so displacing along them reaches genuinely different conformations at low energy cost. Random displacement mostly produces strained structures that are immediately rejected. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation method that runs several constant pH simulations in parallel, each at a different pH or temperature, and periodically swaps configurations between them. The swaps let a configuration stuck in one protonation state escape by way of conditions where that state is unfavourable. It converges protonation populations far faster than a single constant pH run. (UNVERIFIED)

NMR analysis in a simulation context refers to the methods used to calculate NMR-related properties from a molecular dynamics trajectory. This allows for a direct comparison between the simulation results and experimental data from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. This includes calculating observables like J-couplings, nuclear Overhauser effects (NOEs), and relaxation times, which are crucial for validating the accuracy of the simulation.

The r-6 weighted distance averaging is a specific calculation method used in NMR analysis to compute an effective distance from a simulation trajectory that can be directly compared to an experimental nuclear Overhauser effect (NOE). Because the NOE intensity is proportional to the inverse sixth power of the distance between two protons, a simple average of the distance is incorrect. For experts, performing this <r⁻⁶>⁻¹/⁶ averaging is the physically correct way to back-calculate NOE-derived distances from a dynamic ensemble of structures.

This is an enhanced sampling method that combines the replica-exchange method with self-guided Langevin dynamics (SGLD). It runs multiple SGLD simulations in parallel, typically at different temperatures, and attempts to swap their coordinates. This combination aims to leverage the accelerated local exploration of SGLD with the global barrier-crossing capability of replica-exchange for very efficient conformational sampling.

A force field parameterization method is the systematic procedure used to derive the numerical values, or parameters, for a force field. This process involves fitting the parameters of the force field's energy functions to reproduce high-quality data, which can come from quantum mechanical calculations or experimental measurements. For experts, the parameterization method is the core of force field development and determines the accuracy and domain of applicability of the resulting model. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameterization method that derives bond and angle force constants from the matrix of second derivatives of the energy computed quantum mechanically. It projects that matrix onto each bond and angle direction in turn, which separates contributions that a simple fit would confuse. It is the standard way parameters are obtained for a molecule no existing force field covers. (UNVERIFIED)

Temperature replica-exchange molecular dynamics is the standard and most common form of the REMD method. It involves running multiple parallel simulations at a range of different temperatures and attempting to swap their coordinates. This is a robust and widely used method for enhancing the sampling of systems with complex energy landscapes, such as in protein folding simulations.

Well-Tempered Adaptively Biased Molecular Dynamics (WT-ABMD) is an enhanced sampling technique in computational chemistry. It merges the features of adaptively biased molecular dynamics (ABMD) and well-tempered metadynamics to calculate the free energy surface of complex molecular systems while avoiding over-exploration of high-energy states.

A parameterization method in which the molecule's geometry is expressed in internal coordinates, as bond lengths, angles and rotations, and parameters are fitted in those terms. Fitting in internal coordinates makes each parameter correspond to one geometric feature. It is more laborious than fitting in Cartesian coordinates and gives parameters that are easier to interpret and transfer. (UNVERIFIED)

A density fitting method that expands the electron density in spherical harmonic functions centred on each atom, so that electron repulsion integrals can be computed more cheaply. Fitting the density rather than computing every integral exactly is what makes large density functional calculations affordable. The error it introduces is small and controllable. (UNVERIFIED)

A force interpolation method is a numerical technique used in some simulation algorithms to estimate the forces on atoms without calculating them directly at every step. This is often done by calculating the forces on a coarser grid and then interpolating these forces to the actual atomic positions. For experts, this method can be used in some multiple-time-stepping algorithms to reduce the computational cost of the force calculation. (UNVERIFIED)

A temperature control algorithm that changes its own coupling strength as the simulation proceeds. Strong coupling is wanted while a system is still far from its target and unwanted once it has settled, and a fixed setting cannot do both. It adjusts so that the early phase is fast and the later dynamics are left alone. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that governs how a simulation advances and how its physical conditions are held steady. It covers the integrator that moves the atoms forward in time, and the thermostats and barostats that keep temperature and pressure at their targets. These are the algorithms that determine what ensemble a simulation actually samples. (UNVERIFIED)

The use of defined mathematical procedures to process data and extract quantities from it. It covers fitting, transforming, integrating and differentiating the output of a simulation. It is distinguished from the domain-specific analyses by making no assumption about what the numbers represent. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes the force on every atom at each step, from the positions of the atoms and the force field. It dominates the cost of a simulation, because the non-bonded part must consider a great many pairs. Almost every optimisation in a simulation engine is aimed at this step. (UNVERIFIED)

An Ewald summation method in which the charge distribution is represented by charges assigned to atoms by Mulliken population analysis rather than by fixed force field charges. It allows a quantum mechanical charge distribution to be handled by the standard periodic electrostatics machinery. The accuracy is limited by how well atom-centred charges can stand in for the real distribution. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical method for computing energy derivatives in a calculation with more than one quantum layer, such as a high-accuracy method inside a cheaper one. The derivatives of each layer must be combined so that the force on a shared atom is consistent. Getting the combination wrong produces forces that do not match the energy, and a simulation that drifts. (UNVERIFIED)

An application of Ewald summation to a system whose charge distribution comes from a quantum mechanical calculation rather than from fixed charges. It is needed because a quantum region in a periodic box interacts with its own images, which must be accounted for rather than ignored. The difficulty is that the charge distribution changes as the calculation proceeds. (UNVERIFIED)

A multiscale simulation in which a small chemically active region is described by quantum mechanics and the rest by a force field. It is what allows a reaction inside an enzyme to be modelled, since a force field cannot break bonds and a quantum treatment of the whole protein is impossible. The difficulty is always the boundary, where the 2 descriptions must be joined without artefacts. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM method in which the quantum region follows the chemistry, expanding to include whatever is currently involved in the reaction. It differs from a solvent-adaptive scheme in that the region moves with the reactive event rather than merely exchanging solvent. It suits a reaction whose site shifts along a chain or across a surface. (UNVERIFIED)

A general term for a method that calculates the long-range forces in a simulation with periodic boundary conditions, assuming the system is uniform in all directions. It involves summing up the interactions between a particle and all of its periodic images in a way that correctly accounts for the infinite, repeating nature of the simulated system. Standard algorithms like the Ewald sum or Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) are specific implementations of this principle, which is essential for accurately modeling the electrostatics of a bulk liquid. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-isotropic position scaling barostat is a pressure control algorithm that couples the scaling of the x and y dimensions of the simulation box together, while allowing the z dimension to fluctuate independently. This method is specifically designed for simulating planar systems like lipid bilayers, where the pressure in the plane of the membrane is different from the pressure perpendicular to it.

An electrostatic method that computes the force between every pair of charged atoms explicitly and adds them all up. It is exact for a system with no periodic images, and its cost grows with the square of the number of atoms. That growth is why it is used only for small or non-periodic systems. (UNVERIFIED)

Self-guided Langevin dynamics (SGLD) is an enhanced sampling method that accelerates conformational searching by adding a memory-dependent guiding force to the standard equations of motion. This guiding force is calculated from a local average of the forces the system has recently experienced, effectively pushing the system to explore new regions faster. SGLD enhances sampling by reducing random fluctuations and promoting more directed exploration of the potential energy surface.

nodes.lbl: generalized Langevin equation self-guided Langevin dynamics

definition.val: A simulation method that adds a guiding force built from a running average of the system's recent motion, so that slow collective movements are amplified while fast local ones are not. Amplifying the slow motions lets a simulation cross barriers it would otherwise take far longer to reach. Results must be corrected afterwards to recover the unbiased distribution. (UNVERIFIED)

Accelerated molecular dynamics is a special type of simulation whose scope is to overcome the timescale limitations of classical molecular dynamics. It works by adding a "boost" to the system's energy, effectively lowering the energy barriers that separate different molecular conformations. For experts, aMD is an enhanced sampling method that adds a non-negative, history-independent bias potential when the system's potential energy is below a certain threshold, allowing for the recovery of canonical averages through energetic reweighting.

Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) is an enhanced sampling method that speeds up simulations by adding a boost potential that has a Gaussian distribution. This method smooths the potential energy surface, allowing the system to more easily escape from local energy minima.

Ligand Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics is a specific application of the GaMD method focused on enhancing the sampling of a ligand's movement and conformational changes. The boost potential is applied in a way that specifically accelerates the dynamics of the ligand, its binding site, or both.

nodes.lbl: dual-boost ligand Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics

definition.val: Dual-boost ligand Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (Dual-boost LiGaMD) is a variant of the GaMD method where two separate boost potentials are applied simultaneously to enhance the sampling of ligand binding and unbinding pathways. For example, one boost is applied to the dihedral angles of the ligand to enhance its conformational sampling, while a second boost is applied to the total potential energy of the system to accelerate its overall dynamics.

Peptide Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics is a specific application of the GaMD method tailored to enhance the conformational sampling of peptides. The boost potential is applied to accelerate the slow folding and conformational transition events that are characteristic of flexible peptide molecules.

A method that uses probability theory to collect, summarise and draw conclusions from data. It is what puts an uncertainty on a value and what decides whether a difference between 2 results is real. Simulation output is a sample, so nothing taken from it is complete without one. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: dual-boost peptide Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics

definition.val: Dual-boost peptide Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (Dual-boost PepGaMD) is a variant of GaMD where two separate boost potentials are applied simultaneously to enhance the sampling of peptides. One boost is typically applied to the peptide's dihedral angles to accelerate local conformational changes, while the second is applied to the total system potential to overcome larger energy barriers.

Ligand Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics 3 (GaMD3) is a recent and refined version of an enhanced sampling method used to accelerate the simulation of ligand binding and unbinding events. It applies a smoothly varying boost potential to the system's energy landscape, allowing the ligand to escape from deep binding pockets and explore different conformations more rapidly. This third-generation implementation includes improved algorithms for updating the boost potential, aiming for more robust and efficient sampling of complex ligand dynamics.

nodes.lbl: protein-protein interaction Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics

definition.val: This is an application of the GaMD method specifically designed to enhance the sampling of protein-protein binding and unbinding events. The boost potential is applied to the potential energy of the entire complex to accelerate the slow association and dissociation processes.

nodes.lbl: dual-boost protein-protein interaction Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics

definition.val: Dual-boost protein-protein interaction Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (Dual-boost PPI-GaMD) is a variant of GaMD where two separate boost potentials are applied simultaneously to enhance the sampling of protein-protein interfaces. One boost is typically applied to the protein protein interface to accelerate local conformational changes, while the second is applied to the total system potential to overcome larger energy barriers.

Multiply-targeted molecular dynamics is an enhanced sampling technique that biases a simulation to explore the conformational space between several known target structures simultaneously. Unlike standard targeted MD which pulls a molecule from one state to another, this method encourages the system to visit a collection of different functional states. This is useful for characterizing the pathways that connect multiple known conformations of a protein, such as its active and inactive forms.

A Partial Nudged Elastic Band (PNEB) is a computational method used to calculate the minimum energy path for structural transitions. Unlike traditional NEB, it applies the nudging algorithm only to a user-defined subset of atoms while allowing the remaining atoms to optimize freely. This reduces computational costs and supports complex environments like explicit solvents.

An algorithm that searches for the input values giving the best score under some measure, usually the lowest or highest value of a function. In this field the function is almost always an energy and the inputs are atomic positions. The difficulty is that such a search finds the nearest good answer rather than the best one anywhere. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm that adjusts atomic positions to lower the energy of a structure until it reaches a nearby minimum. It moves downhill only, so it settles in the nearest low point rather than the lowest one. It is run on a freshly built system to remove overlaps that would otherwise make the first simulation steps explode. (UNVERIFIED)

A family of minimization algorithms that build up an approximation to the curvature of the energy surface from the slopes seen at successive steps, rather than computing it directly. Reusing past steps this way gives most of the speed of a curvature-based method at the cost of a slope-based one. It is the minimizer AmberTools offers for large systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A lambda-scheduling free energy method is a technique where the alchemical transformation between two states is performed in a single, continuous simulation run. This is achieved by slowly and continuously changing the coupling parameter, lambda, according to a predefined schedule over the course of the simulation. For experts, this non-equilibrium approach can be computationally efficient, and the free energy can be estimated from the work performed during the transformation using fluctuation theorems. (UNVERIFIED)

Hybrid solvent replica-exchange molecular dynamics is a specialized version of the REMD method where the different parallel simulations use different solvent models. For example, some replicas might use an implicit solvent model, which allows for very fast sampling, while others use a more accurate explicit solvent model. Swapping between these replicas allows the simulation to combine the sampling efficiency of implicit solvent with the accuracy of explicit solvent.

Reservoir replica-exchange molecular dynamics is an efficient variant of the REMD method for simulations with a very large number of replicas. Instead of attempting swaps between all adjacent pairs, it attempts swaps between a master simulation and a large "reservoir" of simulations running at different temperatures. This can significantly improve the efficiency of the exchange process when a very wide temperature range needs to be sampled.

Replica-exchange umbrella sampling is an enhanced sampling method that combines two powerful techniques to calculate free energy profiles. It runs multiple umbrella sampling simulations in parallel, each restraining the system to a different window along a reaction coordinate, and periodically attempts to swap the coordinates between these simulations. This combination helps to overcome slow conformational sampling within each umbrella window, leading to faster convergence of the potential of mean force.

nodes.lbl: replica-exchange with arbitrary degree of freedom

definition.val: Replica-exchange with an arbitrary degree of freedom is a powerful generalization of the standard replica-exchange simulation method. Instead of running parallel simulations at different temperatures, this technique allows them to be run along any user-defined variable, such as a reaction coordinate, a force field parameter, or a pH value. By attempting to swap these variables between replicas, the method can dramatically enhance sampling and map out a system's response to a wide range of conditions in a single set of simulations.

A free energy calculation analysis that computes an absolute free energy by thermodynamic integration from a realistic atomistic model to a simplified reference model whose free energy can be solved exactly. The Einstein Molecule model is used for the solute, in which each atom is held in place by a harmonic potential so that the reference free energy has a closed-form solution. EMIL is the name of the module that implements this in AMBER, and its authors call the underlying method Thermodynamic Integration relative to an Exact Solution. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: Berryman J.T. Absolute free energies for biomolecules in implicit or explicit solvent. Physics Procedia, 2014. States that the AMBER implementation of this method is called EMIL.

Berryman J.T. and Schilling T. Free energies by thermodynamic integration relative to an exact solution, used to find the handedness-switching salt concentration for DNA. J. Chem. Theory Comput. 9(1):679-686, 2013.

definition.val: A simulation method in which acidic and basic groups can gain or lose a proton during the run, rather than being fixed at the start. Their protonation is coupled to a chosen acidity, so the populations that result are those at that pH. It matters because a fixed assignment made before the simulation may be wrong, and a wrong charge changes everything downstream. (UNVERIFIED)

A constant pH method in which the degree of protonation of each titratable group is a continuous quantity that moves under its own equation of motion, rather than switching between protonated and deprotonated. Because it changes smoothly, no jump has to be accepted or rejected and the simulation never stops to attempt one. The cost is that intermediate values do not correspond to any real chemical state and must be kept away from. (UNVERIFIED)

Lambda-dynamics is a free energy calculation method where the coupling parameter, lambda, is treated as a dynamic variable that evolves in time, just like an atomic coordinate. A fictitious mass is assigned to lambda, and its "motion" along the transformation pathway is simulated, allowing it to sample different intermediate states.

nodes.lbl: PME continuous constant pH molecular dynamics

definition.val: A continuous constant pH method formulated to work with particle mesh Ewald electrostatics. The difficulty it solves is that changing a charge continuously changes the total charge of the system, which the Ewald treatment assumes is fixed. Without this reformulation, constant pH and the standard long-range electrostatics could not be used together. (UNVERIFIED)

A variational free energy profile method is a class of techniques for finding the minimum free energy path between two states. These methods work by optimizing a trial pathway to minimize a functional that represents the free energy, based on a variational principle. For experts, methods like the string method are a type of variational approach for identifying the most probable transition pathway and the associated free energy barrier. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis method that improves on plain free energy perturbation by applying a weighting function to the sampled configurations. The weighting concentrates effort where the 2 states overlap least, which is where plain perturbation converges worst. It is used when the states are too dissimilar for the unweighted estimator to be reliable. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis method that extends weighted thermodynamic perturbation theory to a broader family of weighting functions. The generalisation lets the weighting be chosen to suit the pair of states rather than taken from a fixed form. It targets the same problem, which is poor overlap between the states being compared. (UNVERIFIED)

Multidimensional replica-exchange molecular dynamics is an extension of the REMD method where exchanges are performed along more than one variable simultaneously. For example, parallel simulations could be run at different temperatures and different pH values, with swaps attempted in both the temperature and pH dimensions.

An optimization algorithm that locates a first-order saddle point on a potential energy surface, where the energy is at a maximum along 1 direction and a minimum along all others. It differs from a minimiser in having to climb in a chosen direction rather than descend in every one. The saddle point it finds is the transition state that sets a reaction barrier. (UNVERIFIED)

A transition state search algorithm that uses 2 closely spaced copies of a structure to find the direction in which the energy curves downwards most, then moves uphill along it to a saddle point. It needs only first derivatives of the energy, never the full matrix of second derivatives. That makes it usable on systems too large for methods that build the whole Hessian. (UNVERIFIED)

A data analysis method that computes the local density, energy and entropy of water on a 3-dimensional grid around a solute, from a simulation with explicit solvent. It assigns thermodynamic quantities to positions rather than to the system as a whole. That is what allows individual hydration sites to be identified and their contribution to solvation free energy to be quantified. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that builds a 3-dimensional map showing which regions around a molecule matter for its function, by computing a chosen property at each point of a grid. What the map shows depends on the property: where a probe binds favourably, where solvent is held, or where charge accumulates. It turns a per-point calculation into a picture that can be inspected. (UNVERIFIED)

An electrostatic method that computes the total electrostatic energy of a periodically repeating system by splitting the calculation into a short-range part summed directly and a long-range part summed in reciprocal space. The split works because each part converges quickly where the other does not. Without it, the sum over periodic images does not converge at all. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes the long-range part of the van der Waals interaction using the same grid-based reciprocal space treatment that particle mesh Ewald applies to electrostatics. Van der Waals forces are usually just cut off at a distance, which introduces a small systematic error in density and surface tension. This removes that error at modest extra cost. (UNVERIFIED)

The part of a force field describing interactions between atoms not joined by a bond, comprising the electrostatic term and the van der Waals term. Every atom in principle interacts with every other, so this part dominates the cost of a simulation. Nearly all the effort of making simulations fast goes into computing it. (UNVERIFIED)

The part of a force field that keeps 4 atoms flat, or preserves a centre's handedness, using a term with a single preferred value rather than a repeating one. The 4 atoms are not in a chain, which is what makes it improper. It exists because the other terms have no way to forbid a planar group from folding. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of mathematical functions, often resembling atomic orbitals, used in quantum chemical calculations to represent the spatial distribution of electrons within a molecule (molecular orbitals). The choice and size of the basis set significantly impact the accuracy and computational cost of a simulation; larger, more flexible basis sets generally yield more accurate results but require more computer resources. These functions serve as the building blocks for constructing the calculated electronic wavefunction. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis method that describes the shape of a 5-membered ring, such as the ribose sugar of a nucleotide, using 2 numbers: the phase angle of pseudorotation and the puckering amplitude. The phase angle says which atoms lie out of the plane and in which direction, and the amplitude says by how much. Together they place a sugar in a named conformational family such as C2'-endo or C3'-endo. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis method that describes the shape of any non-planar ring using a set of numbers derived from how far each atom sits out of the ring's mean plane. It applies to rings of any size, where the older 2-parameter treatment covers 5-membered rings only. For a 6-membered ring it gives 3 numbers that place it on a sphere of possible shapes. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation method in which the forces are adjusted using a function borrowed from machine learning that measures how similar 2 configurations are. The adjustment pushes the system away from configurations it has already visited. That is what encourages it to explore rather than settle. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format defines the specific rules and conventions used to structure, store, and exchange data, particularly within computer files. In biomolecular simulation, this refers to the various standardized ways that information like molecular structures, simulation parameters, or results are organized. Understanding these formats is essential for using simulation software and sharing data. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that provides the necessary data, settings, or instructions required to initiate a computational task. This format provides the instructional input for simulation or analysis software. It is distinct from formats that describe molecular structure or results. (UNVERIFIED)
A data format for a file containing a sequence of commands or code in a specific language. These scripts are designed to be executed by a program to automate a workflow or a series of analysis steps.

A simulation log format is a text-based file structure that records the progress and key information generated during a computer simulation or calculation. It typically includes a copy of the input settings, step-by-step updates on energy and temperature, performance timings, and any warnings or error messages. This format is the primary source for monitoring a simulation's stability, diagnosing problems, and extracting averaged thermodynamic properties after the run is complete.

A category of data formats for files containing information derived from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) experiments. These formats are used to store and exchange experimental data, such as structural restraints, that can be used in simulations.

A data format for a file that stores a complete snapshot of a simulation's state at a specific time. This includes coordinates, velocities, and other state variables sufficient to resume the run. These formats are often binary for efficiency.

A text data format that stores the results of a quantum chemistry calculation for visualization, holding atomic coordinates together with the basis functions and coefficients that describe the molecular orbitals. Because it carries the orbitals themselves rather than only a picture of them, a viewer can render orbitals, electron density and vibrational modes from it. It is read by many visualization programs, not only the one it is named after. (UNVERIFIED)

A simple text-based file format for storing data that exists at various points in 3D space. Each line in the file specifies an x, y, and z coordinate, followed by the data value at that point. It is a straightforward, human-readable format for representing sparse or irregular grid data. (UNVERIFIED)

A script file format for the tleap program in AmberTools, used to build a molecular system for simulation. It contains a sequence of commands to load molecular structures, apply force fields, add solvent, and save the final topology and coordinate files. This format is a fundamental part of the system preparation stage in an Amber workflow. (UNVERIFIED)

The mmCIF format (.cif or .mmcif) is the standard archival format for macromolecular structures used by the Protein Data Bank (PDB), superseding the legacy PDB format. It uses a flexible, dictionary-based syntax (CIF) with key-value pairs and loop structures to store atomic coordinates, connectivity, experimental details, and extensive metadata. It is better suited for handling large, complex structures and diverse experimental data.

The PDB format (.pdb) is the long-standing, fixed-column text format traditionally used for storing protein and nucleic acid structures from the Protein Data Bank. It includes records for metadata, atomic coordinates, and optionally connectivity. While still widely compatible with visualization and simulation software, it is considered obsolete since it has limitations for very large structures and complex metadata compared to the newer mmCIF format.

An identifier is a unique name, code, or label assigned to a specific entity, data record, or concept to distinguish it unambiguously from others within a given context. In scientific databases and computational workflows, identifiers (like accession numbers or unique IDs) are crucial for referencing, retrieving, and linking specific pieces of information accurately. They serve as unique addresses for data points or objects. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A protein database ID is a unique alphanumeric code assigned to each entry in a public protein structure or sequence database, such as the Protein Data Bank (PDB ID, e.g., '1TIM') or UniProt (accession number, e.g., 'P00761'). These identifiers serve as the standard way to reference and retrieve specific protein structures or sequence information.

comments: Retired 2026-08-07 on review by orcid:0000-0002-2294-5393. Two objections, both accepted. First, the Protein Data Bank is not a protein database: it holds nucleic acids, protein-nucleic acid complexes and other assemblies, so the label and definition made a claim that is simply false. Second, a PDB entry identifies a deposited structure while a UniProt accession identifies a sequence record, so grouping them said less than it appeared to. Its two children, MOLSIM:000686 PDB ID and MOLSIM:000687 UniProt ID, were re-parented to MOLSIM:000447 identifier alongside the other identifiers. No IAO:0100001 successor, because there is no single term that replaces it; this is the same shape as the other retired grouping terms whose children were re-parented instead. Note the term had been verified by orcid:0000-0003-4177-3619 before this review.

definition.val: A function that reduces the electrostatic interaction between 2 charges as they approach very closely. Without it, a polarizable model can reach a state where 2 induced dipoles reinforce each other without limit and the energy diverges. Damping prevents that failure, which is called polarization catastrophe. (UNVERIFIED)

Hydrogen bond analysis is a structural analysis method used to identify and quantify the hydrogen bonds that are formed and broken during a simulation. The analysis typically uses a set of geometric criteria, such as a maximum distance between the donor and acceptor atoms and a minimum angle, to define when a hydrogen bond exists.

A structural analysis method that tests whether the orientations of the structures in a collection are spread evenly over all directions. It computes the distribution of orientations and looks for any preferred alignment. It is used to confirm that a simulation has not introduced an artificial bias in rotational motion, which some theoretical treatments assume is absent. (UNVERIFIED)

A dynamics analysis method that breaks the tumbling of a molecule in solution into a set of independent rotational modes. Each mode has its own timescale, so the overall rotation can be described by a few numbers instead of a full trajectory. The result can be compared directly with NMR relaxation measurements. (UNVERIFIED)

Nucleic acid structure analysis is a specialized type of structural analysis that calculates a set of parameters describing the detailed geometry of a DNA or RNA helix, known as the helical parameters. This includes parameters that describe the geometry of individual base pairs as well as the relationship between adjacent base pairs, such as twist, roll, and slide.

A structural analysis method that tracks how many of the atom pairs in contact in a reference folded structure are also in contact at each point in a trajectory. The reference set is taken from the native state and the result is reported as the fraction of it that is present. That fraction is a common single-number measure of how far folding has progressed. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical method that finds the directions in which a system changes most slowly, rather than those in which it varies most. It does this by looking at how coordinates relate to themselves after a delay rather than at the same instant. The slowest motions are usually the functionally important ones, and they are not always the largest. (UNVERIFIED)

A method that decomposes a signal into contributions at different frequencies, while keeping track of when each occurred. A standard frequency analysis says which frequencies are present over the whole record but not when. That matters for a trajectory, where a motion may appear only during part of the run. (UNVERIFIED)

A method that identifies events in a signal from the output of a wavelet decomposition, by finding where energy at a given frequency appears or disappears. It picks out transitions rather than describing the signal as a whole. In a trajectory it marks the moments at which a molecule changed its mode of motion. (UNVERIFIED)

Fluorescence spectroscopy is an experimental technique that measures the light emitted by a substance after it has absorbed light. A molecule absorbs light at one wavelength, promoting it to an excited electronic state, and then emits light at a longer, lower-energy wavelength as it relaxes back down. This technique is highly sensitive and is widely used to study molecular conformation, binding, and dynamics by monitoring changes in the fluorescence signal.

A data format used by GROMACS that defines a reusable template for one residue, giving its atoms, their charges and the bonds between them. It is what lets a topology be built automatically from a sequence rather than written out atom by atom. It is the GROMACS counterpart of the CHARMM residue topology file. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area tool

definition.val: A computational tool or script that implements the MM/PBSA (Molecular Mechanics / Poisson-Boltzmann Surface Area) method for estimating free energy changes, typically ligand binding affinities or solvation free energies. This approach involves calculating molecular mechanics energies (MM), electrostatic solvation free energies using the Poisson-Boltzmann (PB) equation, and non-polar solvation free energies using a term proportional to the Solvent Accessible Surface Area (SASA), usually averaged over snapshots from an MD trajectory. It's an endpoint free energy method, computationally cheaper than FEP or TI but generally considered less rigorous. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area module

definition.val: A molecular mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann surface area tool that is built into a larger simulation or modelling package rather than run on its own. It uses that package's own energy routines and Poisson-Boltzmann solver, which is what distinguishes it from a standalone script such as MMPBSA.py. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: molecular mechanics generalized Born surface area tool

definition.val: A computational tool or script that implements the MM/GBSA (Molecular Mechanics / Generalized Born Surface Area) method for estimating free energy changes, analogous to MM/PBSA. The key difference is that MM/GBSA uses a Generalized Born (GB) model instead of the more computationally expensive Poisson-Boltzmann (PB) equation to calculate the electrostatic contribution to the solvation free energy. Like MM/PBSA, it combines MM energies, GB electrostatic solvation energy, and a SASA-based nonpolar term, averaged over simulation snapshots, providing a faster but often less accurate estimation of binding or solvation free energies compared to rigorous methods. (UNVERIFIED)

A comprehensive molecular similarity measure that combines both shape-based RefTversky and chemical feature-based RefColorTversky scores into a single metric. This combined measure provides a more complete assessment of molecular similarity by considering both geometric shape and chemical functionality simultaneously. The resulting score typically ranges from 0 to 2, though it can occasionally exceed this range due to the field-based nature of shape matching. (UNVERIFIED)

A minimal basis set in which each atomic orbital is approximated by 6 Gaussian functions added together. It is the most faithful imitation in the family and still minimal, so it remains unsuitable for real work. Adding Gaussians improves the shape of each orbital and never lets the electron cloud change shape as a bond forms. (UNVERIFIED)

NModelGB is a specific implementation of a Generalized Born (GB) implicit solvent model, likely used within a particular simulation package. It provides a specific set of equations and parameters for calculating the electrostatic contribution to the solvation free energy. The "NModel" designation distinguishes this particular variant from other GB models available to the user. (UNVERIFIED)

OPM database (Orientations of Proteins in Membranes) is both a database and a web server/tool providing pre-calculated transmembrane orientations and positions for experimentally determined membrane protein structures found in the PDB. OPM uses a computational approach based on minimizing the calculated transfer free energy from water to the lipid bilayer to determine the most likely membrane boundaries and protein position relative to the bilayer center. It's a valuable resource for obtaining initial membrane protein placements for simulations.

Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) is a specific phenomenon in fluorescence spectroscopy where an excited donor fluorophore non-radiatively transfers its energy to a nearby acceptor fluorophore. The efficiency of this energy transfer is extremely sensitive to the distance between the two molecules, making it a "spectroscopic ruler."

A binary file format used to store three-dimensional images or maps, common in electron microscopy. It is the standard format for storing 3D density maps in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and is also used in X-ray crystallography. This format is essential for the visualization and analysis of volumetric data in structural biology. (UNVERIFIED)

A text-based format containing control parameters for the Amber sander and pmemd programs, organized in Fortran namelists. It specifies simulation conditions like timestep, duration, and temperature/pressure coupling algorithms. This format dictates how the molecular dynamics simulation is performed.

A text-based log format generated by Amber's simulation engines that provides a detailed record of the simulation's progress. It contains energy components, thermodynamic properties, and performance timings printed at regular intervals. This format is essential for monitoring simulation stability and extracting averaged properties. (UNVERIFIED)

A format that stores the complete state of an Amber simulation, including atomic coordinates, velocities, and periodic box dimensions. It is used to save the simulation state at a specific point in time, allowing the run to be resumed exactly. The format can be either ASCII-based (.rst7) or binary NetCDF-based (.ncrst).

The Amber molecular dynamics topology file (.prmtop or .parm7) contains all the static information about the molecular system needed for an Amber simulation, excluding coordinates. This includes atom definitions (names, types, masses, charges), molecular connectivity (bonds, angles, dihedrals), force field parameters for all interaction terms, and non-bonded interaction rules. It is generated by programs like tleap and used together with a coordinate file (.inpcrd, .rst7).

A file format generated by the Antechamber program in AmberTools that contains a molecule's structure and atomic properties. It typically stores atom types and partial charges assigned during the parameterization process for a small molecule. This format serves as an intermediate in preparing non-standard molecules for simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational method that predicts how a small molecule sits in a binding site on a protein, and scores how well it binds. It searches over positions and shapes of the molecule and rates each by a scoring function. It is fast enough to screen large libraries, and its scores rank candidates far better than they predict real binding strengths. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular dynamics method that integrates the equations of motion for a coarse-grained model rather than an all-atom one. Fewer and smoother interactions permit a timestep 10 or more times longer, which together with the smaller particle count is where its speed comes from. Its trajectory cannot be interpreted below the size of 1 site. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A specific, widely used 3-point water model type characterized by its simplicity and computational efficiency (Transferable Intermolecular Potential 3-Point). It places charges on the oxygen and two hydrogen atoms and represents water as a rigid molecule with experimentally derived geometry. While computationally fast, it is known to have limitations in reproducing some properties of real water (like the temperature of maximum density or dielectric constant) compared to more complex models.

comments: Retired 2026-08-24 as a duplicate. MOLSIM:000022 TIP3P describes the same rigid three-site model with charges on the oxygen and two hydrogens, and sits with the other 18 water models under MOLSIM:000014 water model force field. This one sat under the parallel MOLSIM:000030 water type branch, which was retired in the same change.

definition.val: A method that assigns charge to atoms by fitting point charges to reproduce the molecule's electrostatic potential at points on a grid outside it. Fitting to the potential is what makes the resulting charges suitable for a force field, since that potential is what other molecules feel. Charges on buried atoms are poorly determined, because the potential outside barely depends on them. (UNVERIFIED)

Molecular surface analysis is a category of analysis methods used to calculate and characterize the surface of a molecule. This includes calculating properties like the total surface area, identifying pockets and cavities, and mapping properties like electrostatic potential onto the surface.

A Connolly surface calculation is a specific algorithm used to compute the solvent-accessible surface of a molecule, which is the surface traced out by the center of a probe sphere as it rolls over the molecule. It is a widely used method for defining the boundary between a molecule and the surrounding solvent.

A covariance matrix calculation is an analysis method that quantifies the correlated motions of atoms in a simulation. The resulting matrix describes how the displacement of each atom is correlated with the displacement of every other atom. For experts, calculating and diagonalizing the covariance matrix is the central step in Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which is used to identify the dominant, large-scale collective motions of a protein or other macromolecule. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. A 2D RMSD analysis is a method where the Root-Mean-Square Deviation (RMSD) is calculated for multiple frames in a simulation trajectory with respect to a reference structure. The reference structure is usually the first frame in the trajectory or an average structure of the whole simulation. The results are typically visualized as a two-dimensional plot, where each point represents the RMSD between one frame and the reference structure.

comments: Retired as redundant with 'RMSD analysis' (MOLSIM:000311), which shares the same parent and the same underlying principle. The 2D frame-to-frame form is now covered explicitly by that term's definition. Reported and approved by the term verifier in GitHub issue #45.

nodes.lbl: lipid SCD order parameter calculation analysis

definition.val: A lipid SCD order parameter calculation is a specific analysis method used to quantify the orientational order of the carbon-hydrogen bonds in the acyl tails of lipid molecules in a membrane simulation. The SCD parameter measures the motional restriction of these bonds relative to the membrane normal. Calculating these order parameters and comparing them to experimental values from NMR is a primary method for validating the accuracy of a membrane simulation.

An analysis method that computes where solvent molecules are likely to sit around a solute by solving integral equations of liquid-state theory on a 3-dimensional grid. It gives a solvent distribution without simulating solvent molecules moving, so no sampling problem arises. What it cannot give is any individual solvent molecule's behaviour over time. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM method in which solvent molecules pass between the quantum and the classical region as they diffuse, rather than being assigned once. A fixed assignment would either trap particular water molecules in the quantum region or cut them as they moved out. The method exists because solvent does not stay put. (UNVERIFIED)

A basis set that represents each valence orbital with 2 or more functions of different spatial extent, while keeping a single function for each core orbital. The extra valence functions let the electron cloud expand or contract as bonding requires, which a minimal set cannot. Splitting only the valence shell concentrates the added cost where bonding happens. (UNVERIFIED)

A split-valence Gaussian basis set describing each core orbital with 3 contracted primitives and each valence orbital with 2 functions, built from 2 and 1 primitives. It is small enough for large molecules and crude enough that its geometries are only approximate. It is used for a quick first optimisation before a better basis set is applied. (UNVERIFIED)

A split-valence Gaussian basis set describing each core orbital with 4 contracted primitives and each valence orbital with 2 functions. It differs from the 3-primitive version only in the description of the core, which barely affects bonding. It is rarely used today. (UNVERIFIED)

An improper torsion potential in which the energy rises with the square of the departure from a single preferred value. Unlike the repeating cosine form it has one minimum, which is what makes it suitable for holding a group flat. The AMBER force fields use a cosine form for the same purpose, so the 2 conventions are not interchangeable. (UNVERIFIED)

A potential energy function representing the van der Waals interaction between 2 atoms, with a steep repulsion at short range and a weaker attraction falling off with the sixth power of distance. The attraction has a physical basis in dispersion; the repulsion is chosen for computational convenience rather than derived. It is the form almost every force field uses. (UNVERIFIED)

A software program that prepares, corrects and checks a molecular structure before it is used in a simulation. Its tasks include adding atoms the experimental structure does not contain, choosing between alternative positions where the data was ambiguous, and reporting geometry that cannot be right. Experimental structures nearly always need this, because crystallography rarely sees hydrogens and often misses flexible loops. (UNVERIFIED)

A comprehensive commercial molecular modeling software suite developed by Certara, widely used in drug discovery and computational chemistry. SYBYL offers extensive tools for structure building and manipulation, conformational analysis, pharmacophore modeling, QSAR, docking, scoring, and visualization, along with molecular mechanics and dynamics capabilities. It provides an integrated environment for many structure preparation and modeling tasks relevant to biomolecular simulation setup, particularly in pharmaceutical research. (UNVERIFIED)

A visualization and analysis program for protein structures that also performs measurement, superposition and simple modelling. It can build a model of one protein on the structure of a related one, and submit that model for refinement. It is now distributed under the name DeepView, which should be kept as an exact synonym of this term. (UNVERIFIED)

A very popular, powerful, and widely used open-source (with some subscription features) molecular visualization system, known for producing high-quality 3D images of molecules and biological macromolecules. PyMOL allows detailed structure inspection, analysis (measurements, surfaces, electrostatics), creating publication-quality figures and animations, and includes scripting capabilities for automation. It is an indispensable tool for visualizing simulation setups and trajectories, although its structure manipulation capabilities are less extensive than dedicated modeling suites. (UNVERIFIED)

Minimization is a computational step that relaxes a molecular structure to remove any bad clashes between atoms. As a stage of the preparation process, energy minimization is a procedure that adjusts the atomic coordinates to find a nearby local minimum on the potential energy surface, thereby removing steric strain from the initial model. This is achieved by using algorithms like steepest descent or conjugate gradient to iteratively reduce the net forces on the atoms until a convergence criterion, such as grms_tol, is met. This process is referred to in log files and inputs with terms like "MINIMIZATION," "ntmin=1," "emtol," and "ncyc." (UNVERIFIED)

An empirically derived set of atomic radii developed by Sitkoff, Sharp, and Honig in the 1990s, specifically optimized for use in continuum electrostatic calculations, particularly Poisson-Boltzmann (PB) calculations aimed at reproducing experimental solvation energies (PARSE stands for "Parameters for Solvation Energy"). These radii define the boundary between the low-dielectric solute molecule and the high-dielectric solvent continuum in PB theory. They differ significantly from standard Van der Waals radii (like Bondi's) as they are optimized to implicitly account for various energetic contributions within that specific theoretical framework (PB/SA). (UNVERIFIED)

A Python library that implements the multi-state Bennett acceptance ratio estimator for combining data from simulations at several thermodynamic states. It returns free energy differences between any pair of those states together with equilibrium averages. It is the reference implementation most other tools call. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical metric used to judge how well a computational method performs, rather than to describe the system being studied. Error measures, correlation measures and ranking measures all belong here. They are what a method is validated against before its predictions are relied on. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical metric that rates how useful a model's predictions are for making a decision, by weighting each pair of compounds by how much choosing wrongly between them would cost. It counts a wrong ordering of 2 very different compounds more heavily than of 2 similar ones. It is used where a model is meant to guide a choice rather than reproduce a number. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: accuracy of ddG prediction metrics measurements analysis

definition.val: A data analysis method that measures how closely predicted relative binding free energies match experimental ones for the same set of ligand pairs. It reports error measures such as root mean square error and mean absolute error, and agreement measures such as the Pearson correlation and the Kendall rank correlation. The rank measures matter most when the purpose is to order ligands rather than to predict a number. (UNVERIFIED)

A QM/MM scheme in which the quantum region is computed in isolation and its interaction with the surroundings is treated entirely by the force field. The quantum region therefore never feels the charges around it, so its electron distribution does not respond to its environment. It is the simplest scheme and the least accurate where the environment is polar. (UNVERIFIED)

A split-valence Gaussian basis set describing each core orbital with 4 contracted primitives and each valence orbital with 2 functions built from 3 and 1 primitives. It was an early step towards the widely used 6-31G family and is superseded by it. It is retained because older published work used it. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical mathematical technique used to assess whether an observed linear relationship (correlation) between two variables, calculated from simulation data, is statistically meaningful. It evaluates the probability that such a correlation could have occurred simply by random chance if no true underlying relationship existed. This helps researchers confidently interpret potential connections found in simulation results. (UNVERIFIED)

A common specific method for linear correlation significance determination (and statistical testing in general) that involves calculating a probability value, the p-value. The p-value represents the probability of observing the calculated correlation, or a stronger one, assuming that there is actually no real correlation (the null hypothesis). A small p-value (typically below a threshold like 0.05) leads to the conclusion that the observed correlation is statistically significant and unlikely due to chance. (UNVERIFIED)

A split-valence Gaussian basis set describing each core orbital with 6 contracted primitives and each valence orbital with 2 functions. The larger core description makes it more accurate than its 3-primitive and 4-primitive relatives for core-dependent properties and no better for bonding. It is rarely used today. (UNVERIFIED)

A split-valence Gaussian basis set that describes each core orbital with 6 contracted primitives and each valence orbital with 2 functions, an inner one contracted from 3 primitives and an outer one from a single primitive. It is one of the most widely used basis sets in quantum chemistry, because it is far more accurate than a minimal basis set while staying cheap enough for routine work. It is also the starting point most polarization and diffuse variants are built on. (UNVERIFIED)

A multiscale method that describes a solute quantum mechanically while representing the surrounding solvent with a generalized Born continuum model. The quantum region can then respond electronically to the solvent without any solvent molecules being simulated. It is used where reactivity matters but explicit solvent would be too expensive. (UNVERIFIED)

A time-averaged restraint simulation is an advanced simulation method where the restraining potential is applied not to the instantaneous structure, but to the average of a an experimental one over a period of time. This is particularly useful for incorporating experimental data, like from NMR, which is also an average over time and a molecular ensemble. For experts, this method provides a more physically meaningful way to enforce experimental restraints that reflect the dynamic nature of the molecule.

A split-valence Gaussian basis set that describes each core orbital with 6 contracted primitives and each valence orbital with 3 functions of different spatial extent, contracted from 3, 1 and 1 primitives. The extra valence function gives more freedom than a double-split set, so it is more accurate for the same molecule. It is usually used together with polarization and diffuse functions rather than on its own. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of effective core potentials and matching valence basis sets developed at Los Alamos National Laboratory for calculations on heavier elements. The potential replaces the chemically inert inner electrons with a single function, which cuts cost and folds in some relativistic effects, while the valence basis describes the electrons that form bonds. It is the successor to the older LANL2 family. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of effective core potentials and valence basis sets from the Los Alamos LANL08 family, with f type polarization functions added on the heavy atoms the potential covers. The f functions give more freedom in describing electron distribution, which matters for bonding in molecules containing heavier elements. (UNVERIFIED)

A Los Alamos effective core potential paired with a valence basis contracted to 6 s-type, 4 p-type, 4 d-type and 2 f-type functions. The potential replaces the inner electrons, and the large valence contraction gives far more flexibility than the standard double-zeta basis of the same family. It is used for heavier elements where the standard basis is too small to describe bonding accurately. (UNVERIFIED)

A Los Alamos effective core potential paired with a double-zeta valence basis, for elements from the third row onwards. The potential replaces the inner electrons with a single function, which cuts cost and folds in some relativistic effects. It is the most widely used effective core potential basis combination. (UNVERIFIED)

A Los Alamos effective core potential with a double-zeta valence basis, carrying 1 extra d type and 1 extra f type polarization function on the heavy atoms the potential covers. The higher angular momentum functions give the valence basis more freedom, which improves the description of bonding for heavier elements. (UNVERIFIED)

A Los Alamos effective core potential with a double-zeta valence basis, carrying 2 additional s, p, d and f functions on the heavy atoms the potential covers. The additions give far more freedom in describing valence electrons than the standard double-zeta set. (UNVERIFIED)

A Los Alamos effective core potential with a double-zeta valence basis, carrying d type polarization functions on the heavy atoms the potential covers and p type polarization functions on hydrogen. The added polarization functions improve molecular geometries and interaction energies markedly over the unpolarized version. (UNVERIFIED)

A Los Alamos effective core potential with a double-zeta valence basis, carrying d type polarization functions on the heavy atoms the potential covers and p type polarization functions on hydrogen. The added polarization functions improve molecular geometries and interaction energies markedly over the unpolarized version. (UNVERIFIED)

A Los Alamos effective core potential paired with a triple-zeta valence basis set, using 3 functions per valence orbital. The extra valence function makes it more flexible and more accurate than the double-zeta member of the same family, at a higher cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A Los Alamos effective core potential with a triple-zeta valence basis set, with f type polarization functions added on the heavy atoms the potential covers. The f functions describe electron correlation and polarization around heavier elements more accurately than the unaugmented set. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set giving 2 functions per valence orbital with a set of polarization functions. It is the smallest member of its family and the cheapest at which correlated methods give meaningful results. It is used as the lowest point of an extrapolation towards the complete basis set limit. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 3 functions per valence orbital together with polarization functions up to f type. It is the level at which correlated calculations first become reliably useful. It is the most widely used member of the family. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 4 functions per valence orbital together with polarization functions up to g type. It is used where a triple-zeta result is not converged enough, and as one point in an extrapolation to the complete basis set limit. Its cost restricts it to modest-sized molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 5 functions per valence orbital together with polarization functions up to h type. It is built for benchmark calculations that need to come very close to the complete basis set limit for correlation energy. Its cost restricts it to small systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 6 functions per valence orbital together with polarization functions up to i type. It is 1 step larger than the quintuple-zeta set and buys a further small step towards the complete basis set limit. In practice it is feasible only for atoms and diatomic molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 8 functions per valence orbital together with very extensive polarization functions. It exists to study how results converge towards the complete basis set limit, rather than to be used in ordinary work. Its cost restricts it to single atoms and diatomic molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 9 functions per valence orbital together with polarization functions of very high angular momentum. It is among the largest sets ever constructed in this family and serves only to extrapolate towards the complete basis set limit. It is too expensive for any molecular calculation. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the correlation-consistent double-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It approximates products of orbital basis functions rather than representing orbitals itself. Pairing it with a different orbital basis degrades the approximation it was fitted for. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the correlation-consistent triple-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It approximates products of orbital basis functions so integrals can be evaluated faster. It is not used to represent orbitals. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the correlation-consistent quadruple-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It carries the extra functions that fitting products of the larger orbital basis requires. Its purpose is speed, not accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the correlation-consistent quintuple-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It is not used to represent orbitals; it approximates products of them so that integrals can be evaluated faster. Without it, calculations at that orbital basis size are often impractical. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the correlation-consistent sextuple-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It approximates products of orbital basis functions rather than the orbitals themselves. It is what allows benchmark calculations at that orbital basis size to run at all. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at double-zeta level that adds tight functions, of large exponent, to describe correlation involving the core electrons. Standard valence sets assume the core is inert, which is a poor approximation for properties that depend on core-valence correlation. It is the smallest member of the family and the cheapest at which the effect can be seen at all. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at triple-zeta level that adds tight functions, of large exponent, to describe correlation involving the core electrons. Standard valence sets assume the core is inert, which is a poor approximation for properties that depend on core-valence correlation. It is the level at which core-valence correlation is usually first worth its cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at quadruple-zeta level that adds tight functions, of large exponent, to describe correlation involving the core electrons. Standard valence sets assume the core is inert, which is a poor approximation for properties that depend on core-valence correlation. It is used for benchmark work where core-valence correlation must be converged rather than merely included. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at quintuple-zeta level that adds tight functions describing correlation involving the core electrons, without diffuse functions. It is used for benchmark work where core-valence correlation must be converged. Its size restricts it to very small systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at sextuple-zeta level that adds tight functions describing correlation involving the core electrons, without diffuse functions. It is among the largest such sets in existence and approaches the complete basis set limit for the core-valence contribution. Its size restricts it to atoms and diatomic molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent double-zeta basis set carrying 1 extra energy-optimised d type polarization function beyond the standard set. The extra function was added because the standard double-zeta set was found short of d functions for the second-row elements sodium to argon. For first-row elements it behaves like the ordinary double-zeta set. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent triple-zeta basis set carrying 1 extra optimised d type polarization function beyond the standard set. It describes polarization and correlation for the second-row elements sodium to argon more completely than the ordinary triple-zeta set. For other elements the 2 are equivalent. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent quadruple-zeta basis set carrying 1 extra optimised d type polarization function beyond the standard set. It is used for benchmark-quality results on the second-row elements sodium to argon, where d function flexibility limits accuracy. For other elements the 2 are equivalent. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent quintuple-zeta basis set carrying 1 extra optimised d type polarization function beyond the standard set. It is used in high-level benchmark work on small molecules containing the second-row elements sodium to argon. For other elements the 2 are equivalent. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent sextuple-zeta basis set carrying 1 extra optimised d type polarization function beyond the standard set. It is a highly specialised set for work on the second-row elements sodium to argon near the complete basis set limit. For other elements the 2 are equivalent. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set giving 2 functions per valence orbital, with 1 diffuse function added at each angular momentum present. The diffuse functions matter for anions, weakly bound complexes and response properties. It is the smallest basis set at which such properties can be attempted. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set giving 3 functions per valence orbital, with a set of diffuse functions added. It is the usual working choice where both correlation and diffuse character matter. It is large enough to be trusted and small enough for molecules of a few dozen atoms. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set giving 4 functions per valence orbital with a set of diffuse functions added at each angular momentum. The diffuse functions matter for anions, weakly bound complexes and response properties. It is a common point in an extrapolation towards the complete basis set limit. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 5 functions per valence orbital and adds a set of diffuse functions. The diffuse functions matter when electron density reaches far from the nuclei, as in an anion or a weakly bound complex. It is a benchmark-level set and its cost limits it to very small systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 6 functions per valence orbital and adds a set of diffuse functions. It is one of the largest standard augmented sets available. It is used to study convergence, or for properties that need extreme accuracy in both correlation and diffuse electron density. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 8 functions per valence orbital and adds a set of diffuse functions. It is a research set used almost only on atoms and diatomic molecules, to study how properties sensitive to diffuse electrons converge. It is not usable for molecular calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set that gives 9 functions per valence orbital and adds a set of diffuse functions. Like the octuple-zeta version it is a research set for atoms and diatomic molecules only. It is not usable for molecular calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the diffuse-augmented correlation-consistent double-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It carries the extra functions needed to fit products involving the diffuse part of that basis. Pairing it with a different orbital basis degrades the approximation it was fitted for. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the diffuse-augmented correlation-consistent triple-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It carries the extra functions needed to fit products involving the diffuse part of that basis. Pairing it with a different orbital basis degrades the approximation it was fitted for. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the diffuse-augmented correlation-consistent quadruple-zeta orbital basis in density fitting calculations. It carries the extra functions needed to fit products involving the diffuse part of that basis. Its purpose is speed, not accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the diffuse-augmented correlation-consistent quintuple-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It carries the extra functions needed to fit products involving the diffuse part of that orbital basis. Its purpose is speed, not accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

An auxiliary basis set built to be paired with the diffuse-augmented correlation-consistent sextuple-zeta orbital basis in resolution-of-identity or density fitting calculations. It is required in practice, because calculations at that orbital basis size are otherwise not feasible. Its purpose is speed, not accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at double-zeta level that adds both diffuse functions and tight functions describing correlation involving the core electrons. Standard valence sets assume the core is inert, which fails for properties that depend on it. It is the smallest combination that carries both additions. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at triple-zeta level that adds both diffuse functions and tight functions describing correlation involving the core electrons. Standard valence sets assume the core is inert, which fails for properties that depend on it. It is the usual working choice where a system needs diffuse character and core-valence correlation at once. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at quadruple-zeta level that adds both diffuse functions and tight functions describing correlation involving the core electrons. Standard valence sets assume the core is inert, which fails for properties that depend on it. It is used where both effects must be converged rather than merely present. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at quintuple-zeta level that adds both diffuse functions and tight functions describing correlation involving the core electrons. Standard valence sets assume the core is inert, which fails for properties that depend on it. It is a benchmark set whose cost restricts it to small systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A correlation-consistent basis set at sextuple-zeta level that adds both diffuse functions and tight functions describing correlation involving the core electrons. Standard valence sets assume the core is inert, which fails for properties that depend on it. It is among the largest standard basis sets in existence and is confined to atoms and diatomic molecules. (UNVERIFIED)
