The ion can then exchange its surroundings freely, as a real ion in solution does. It cannot reproduce the fixed geometry of a metal held in a protein site. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-bonded potential that adds a term falling off with the fourth power of distance to the usual repulsion and attraction, representing the ion polarizing the molecules around it. That extra attraction is what a fixed-charge model otherwise omits entirely for a highly charged ion. It lets one parameter set reproduce both an ion's hydration energy and its ion-water distance, which the standard form cannot. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvation model in which the solute is surrounded by a spherical droplet of explicit water rather than a fully periodic box. Using a droplet cuts the number of water molecules sharply, which is the whole purpose. It introduces a free surface, where water behaves unlike bulk, so results near the edge of the droplet are unreliable. (UNVERIFIED)

A representation of a single molecule as a set of atoms together with the rules governing how they interact. It fixes what is represented explicitly and what is left out, such as whether hydrogens appear individually. It is the unit a simulated system is assembled from. (UNVERIFIED)

A model in which a molecule is represented as a set of independent harmonic oscillators, each vibrating about a fixed position. It is not meant to describe any real molecule; it serves as a reference state whose free energy is known exactly. That known value is what absolute free energies of solids and of bound states are measured against. (UNVERIFIED)

An implicit solvent model that approximates the electrostatic part of the solvation free energy with a closed-form expression, using an effective radius for each atom that reflects how deeply it is buried. It avoids solving a partial differential equation, so it is fast enough to run inside a simulation rather than only afterwards. Its accuracy rests entirely on how those effective radii are computed. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that refines the neck correction to the effective Born radii with re-fitted parameters. It reproduces Poisson-Boltzmann solvation energies more closely than the earlier neck model. It is the version recommended for folding and for intrinsically disordered systems. (UNVERIFIED)

An experimental refinement model is a computational model used to improve or interpret raw experimental data, particularly in structural biology. It combines a theoretical energy function, like a molecular mechanics force field, with terms that represent the experimental observations, such as X-ray diffraction patterns or NMR restraints.

A model of the disordered solvent in a crystal, used during experimental structure refinement to account for the scattering that ordered atoms do not explain. It treats that solvent as a uniform continuum of constant electron density rather than as individual water molecules. Without it, the low-resolution terms of a diffraction pattern cannot be fitted. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-bonded potential energy function modified so that the energy stays finite when 2 atoms overlap completely. It removes the singularity in the Lennard-Jones and Coulomb terms that appears as an atom is created or annihilated in an alchemical calculation. Without it the calculation becomes numerically unstable near the end points of the coupling parameter. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field in which the total energy is the sum of independent terms, each depending on a fixed set of atoms and unaffected by the rest of the system. Independence is what makes the energy cheap to compute and easy to parallelise. It also means the parameters cannot respond to their environment, which is what a polarizable force field adds. (UNVERIFIED)

A model that describes a system through the probabilities of its possible microscopic arrangements, rather than by following any one of them. It connects what individual particles do to the temperature, pressure and free energy that are actually measured. Every thermodynamic quantity taken from a simulation rests on one. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: Not to be confused with STATO:0000107 "statistical model", which is a statistics and inference concept: a formalization of relationships between random variables. This term is the statistical-MECHANICS sense - the theoretical framework connecting the microscopic motion of atoms to macroscopic thermodynamic properties, for example the canonical ensemble. Renamed 2026-07-29 to remove that ambiguity; "statistical model" is retained as an exact synonym.

definition.val: A statistical model giving how the speeds of particles are spread at a given temperature, when the system is at thermal equilibrium. Most particles move near an average speed, with a long tail of fast ones and few very slow ones. Starting velocities in a simulation are drawn from it, and the observed distribution is checked against it to confirm the system has equilibrated. (UNVERIFIED)

A two-state transition model is a simplified statistical mechanics model used to describe a system that can exist in two distinct states, such as a protein in a folded or unfolded state. The model characterizes the probability of switching from one state to the other, often used to analyze the kinetics of conformational changes.

A scheme for building the grid of points on which a density functional theory calculation is integrated, by giving each atom its own spherical grid and blending them with weights that sum to 1 everywhere. The blending avoids double counting where atomic grids overlap. It is the standard construction such grids are built by. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of points and weights on a sphere chosen so that a numerical integration over that sphere is exact for spherical harmonics up to a stated order. It reaches a given accuracy with far fewer points than an evenly spaced grid. It is the angular part of the grid a density functional theory calculation integrates on. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid 3-site water model refitted from its predecessor to reproduce measured properties of biomolecules in water rather than of bulk water alone. The refit adjusts how strongly water interacts with a solute. It exists because a model fitted to pure water does not necessarily solvate a protein correctly. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid 3-site water model refitted from its predecessor against a wide set of measured properties simultaneously, rather than a few. Fitting to many targets at once gives better agreement across temperature and pressure than fitting to a handful. It keeps the 3-site form, so it costs no more than the model it replaces. (UNVERIFIED)

A rigid 3-site water model whose charges and geometry were chosen to reproduce the measured electrostatic moments of a water molecule in the liquid, rather than being fitted directly to bulk properties. Getting those moments right makes the bulk properties follow. It reproduces more measured quantities than other 3-site models at the same cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A 3-site water model that adjusts its charge distribution in response to the electric field around it. Real water is markedly more polar in the liquid than as an isolated molecule, and a fixed-charge model must compromise between the 2. A polarizable model does not have to, at several times the cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A coarse-grained water model in which 1 interaction bead stands for 4 real water molecules. Reducing the solvent particle count fourfold is where most of the speed of a coarse-grained simulation comes from, because solvent dominates the atom count. It is used with coarse-grained force fields such as MARTINI. (UNVERIFIED)

A crystallographic model component is a fundamental concept used to describe the structure of a crystal. It represents one of the key pieces of information, such as the repeating unit or the symmetry rules, that define how molecules are arranged in a crystalline solid.

The smallest portion of a crystal from which the whole structure can be built by applying the symmetry operations of its space group. It may hold 1 molecule, several, or a fraction of 1, depending on where the molecules sit relative to the symmetry elements. It is what a deposited crystal structure file usually contains. (UNVERIFIED)

A solvation shell refers to the layer of solvent molecules that are in direct contact with or in the immediate vicinity of a solute molecule. These solvent molecules are often more ordered and have different dynamic properties compared to the bulk solvent further away. Usually, analyzing the structure and dynamics of the first and second solvation shells is crucial for understanding the details of solute-solvent interactions.

A way of describing the 3-dimensional arrangement of atoms in a molecule, either as Cartesian coordinates or as internal coordinates such as bond lengths, angles and dihedral angles. The 2 carry the same information but behave differently: internal coordinates make a constraint or a symmetry easy to impose, Cartesian ones make a translation or a rotation trivial. The choice is usually dictated by the program. (UNVERIFIED)

A way of describing a molecule's geometry by giving each atom's position relative to atoms already placed, as a bond length, an angle and a rotation. It expresses shape directly, so a symmetry or a constraint can be imposed by fixing one number. It becomes unstable when 3 atoms it refers to lie nearly in a straight line. (UNVERIFIED)

The collection of fitted numbers that gives a force field its behaviour for a particular class of molecules, such as proteins, lipids or carbohydrates. The functional form stays the same across sets; the numbers change. A simulation states both the form and the set, because the form alone does not identify what was used. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter set covering phosphorylated amino acids such as phosphoserine, phosphothreonine and phosphotyrosine, for use alongside the ff10 protein force field. Standard protein parameters do not include them, because phosphorylation is a modification rather than a standard residue. It is matched to that protein force field and should not be used with another. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter set covering phosphorylated amino acids such as phosphoserine, phosphothreonine and phosphotyrosine, for use alongside the ff14SB protein force field. Standard protein parameters do not include them, because phosphorylation is a modification rather than a standard residue. It is matched to that protein force field and should not be used with another. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter set covering phosphorylated amino acids such as phosphoserine, phosphothreonine and phosphotyrosine, for use alongside the ff19SB protein force field. Standard protein parameters do not include them, because phosphorylation is a modification rather than a standard residue. It is matched to that protein force field and should not be used with another. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of parameters for common single-atom ions, fitted separately for each of several water models. Fitting per water model is the point: parameters that behave correctly with one water model do not with another. Using them with a water model they were not fitted for gives wrong hydration and wrong ion pairing. (UNVERIFIED)

A collection of mathematical functions combined to represent the shape of each electron orbital in a quantum chemistry calculation. The true orbitals cannot be written down, so they are built up from a finite set of simpler functions instead. Everything a calculation can and cannot describe follows from which functions are in that set. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of mathematical functions used to approximate products of orbital basis functions, rather than the orbitals themselves, so that electron repulsion integrals can be computed more cheaply. It is what makes density fitting and resolution-of-identity methods fast. It must be matched to the orbital basis set it is paired with, or the speed-up costs accuracy. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter set extending the standard lipid parameters to cover lipid species they do not include. It is used when a membrane contains a lipid the main parameter set was never fitted for. Parameters obtained this way are less well tested than those in the main set. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of machine learning force field that combines a deep neural network for short-range atomic interactions with a classical physics-based function for long-range interactions. The neural network is trained on high-accuracy quantum mechanics data to learn the complex, many-body interactions at short distances. This hybrid approach leverages the power of machine learning for the most difficult part of the calculation while retaining an efficient and physically correct description of the long-range forces, such as electrostatics. (UNVERIFIED)

A description of the full symmetry of a crystal, listing the rotations, reflections, translations and their combinations that leave the structure unchanged. There are 230 such groups in 3 dimensions, and every crystal belongs to exactly 1. Together with the asymmetric unit it determines the entire crystal. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that computes effective Born radii with the scheme of Onufriev, Bashford and Case. Its radii agree closely with Poisson-Boltzmann results at a small fraction of the cost. It is the default implicit solvent in AMBER and the most widely used member of this family. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that corrects the effective Born radii for the narrow regions between overlapping atomic spheres, which earlier formulations treated as more solvent-exposed than they are. The correction matters most in crevices and buried pockets. The letter n in the name stands for those neck regions. (UNVERIFIED)

A label classifying an atom by its element and its local bonding environment, in the scheme used by the SYBYL software and by the Mol2 file format. It distinguishes, for instance, an aromatic carbon from a carbon in a double bond. It is the classification most cheminformatics tools read from a structure file. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized distance coordinate restraint is a type of restraint that is applied to a complex coordinate defined as a combination of multiple distances, angles, or dihedrals. This allows for the restraining of complex conformational changes, such as the movement of a whole domain, that cannot be described by a single distance.

An electronic property giving how a molecule's electrons respond to a magnetic field, as a 3-by-3 array because the response depends on the field's direction relative to the molecule. A molecule with circulating electrons, such as an aromatic ring, responds much more strongly along one axis than the others. It is what underlies the ring current shifts seen in NMR spectra. (UNVERIFIED)

An alignment tensor is a mathematical object that describes the degree and direction of the average orientation of molecules in a sample that is not perfectly random. In an NMR experiment, molecules can be weakly aligned by a magnetic field, and the alignment tensor quantifies this small but measurable preference in orientation. This tensor is crucial for interpreting experimental data like residual dipolar couplings (RDCs), which provide powerful long-range structural information.

A pair of numbers defining the van der Waals interaction of an atom type: one giving how strongly it is attracted and one giving its effective size. Parameters for 2 different atom types are combined by a rule specific to each force field. Those combining rules differ between force fields, which is one reason their parameters cannot be mixed. (UNVERIFIED)

An implicit solvent model that represents a solute as a low-dielectric cavity in a high-dielectric continuum and solves for the electrostatic potential, including the screening by mobile salt ions. It makes no analytical approximation to the molecule's shape, so it is the reference the faster models are judged against. Solving it numerically is expensive, which is why it is usually applied to snapshots rather than during a simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A Poisson-Boltzmann model in which the equation is linearized and solved in closed form under simplifying assumptions about geometry. It is far faster than solving the full non-linear equation numerically. It holds only where electrostatic potentials are small, so it is unreliable for highly charged systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that accounts for charge hydration asymmetry, the fact that a negative ion and a positive ion of the same size are not solvated equally by water. It adjusts the solvation term according to the sign of the charge, which a standard generalized Born model cannot do. It was built to improve solvation free energies for ions. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model whose effective Born radii for ions were re-fitted to reproduce measured hydration free energies. It targets the ions specifically, leaving the treatment of the solute unchanged. It is used where ion solvation must be right but explicit water is too expensive. (UNVERIFIED)

A generalized Born implicit solvent model that computes each atom's effective radius from an analytical integral over the molecular surface rather than over atomic volumes. Integrating over the surface reproduces Poisson-Boltzmann results more closely, particularly for buried atoms. It is built for accuracy at a cost still far below solving the Poisson-Boltzmann equation. (UNVERIFIED)

A model that estimates the free energy of a process by adding up tabulated free energies for moving each chemical group between environments, such as from water into a protein interior. The group values are measured once on small molecules and then reused. It is fast and additive, which also means it cannot capture effects that depend on how groups are arranged relative to one another. (UNVERIFIED)

A database holding the 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional structures of small organic compounds. Such collections supply the starting geometries and the reference conformations that force field parameters are fitted and tested against. They differ from protein structure archives in holding many small entries rather than few large ones. (UNVERIFIED)

A RISM model that solves the integral equations on a 3-dimensional grid around a solute, giving the spatial distribution of each solvent site. It shows where solvent molecules are likely to sit, including individual ordered water positions, without running a simulation. It needs the bulk solvent correlation functions from a 1-dimensional calculation as input. (UNVERIFIED)

An approximate equation relating the 2 unknown correlation functions in an integral equation theory of liquids, so that the system can be solved. Without it there are 2 unknowns and 1 equation. Different choices, such as hypernetted-chain or Kovalenko-Hirata, give measurably different solvation free energies from otherwise identical input. (UNVERIFIED)

The Kovalenko-Hirata (KH) closure is a mathematical approximation used in the statistical mechanical Ornstein-Zernike (OZ) integral equation theory (commonly utilized in 3D-RISM theory) to calculate solvent structure and solvation free energy.

An implicit solvent model that predicts solvation free energy with a model trained on more expensive calculations, using the shape of the surface the solvent cannot enter. It replaces the analytical approximation that a generalized Born model makes with a fitted one. It is faster than solving the Poisson-Boltzmann equation and more accurate than the analytical approximations, within the range it was trained on. (UNVERIFIED)

A machine-learned potential that predicts only the difference between a cheap approximate calculation and an accurate one, rather than the full energy. The difference is smaller and smoother than the energy itself, so far less training data is needed to learn it well. The cheap calculation still has to be run, which is the cost of the approach. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge model that fits permanent point charges to the electrostatic potential and adds an induced dipole on each atom to represent the response to a field. The permanent part describes the isolated molecule and the induced part its response to the environment. It is how a polarizable force field is parameterised from quantum calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

A charge model that fits a dipole and higher terms on each atom, not only a point charge, to reproduce the electrostatic potential around a molecule. The extra terms capture features a point charge cannot, such as the anisotropy of a lone pair or the positive region on a halogen. It is more accurate and more expensive to use. (UNVERIFIED)

The AMBER FB15 (force-balanced 15) protein force field is a refinement of the AMBER94 ff with a systematic and thorough optimization of the intramolecular terms. The key difference in the optimized result is a significant lowering of the potential in regions away from the energy minima, which is expected to yield greater flexibility in finite temperature simulations. This force field is particularly useful for simulations of proteins, particularly when fluctuations away from equilibrium, conformational changes, and/or temperature dependence are expected to play important roles.

A force field in which non-polar hydrogens are merged into the heavy atom they are bonded to, so that a methyl group is one interaction site. It roughly halves the atom count of an organic system at little cost in accuracy, because those hydrogens carry almost no charge. Polar hydrogens are kept, because they form hydrogen bonds. (UNVERIFIED)

A light charged particle attached by a spring to an atom, used to represent how that atom's electron cloud shifts in an electric field. The particle moves with the field while the atom stays put, which reproduces polarization without any electrons being modelled. Treating polarization as an extra particle lets an ordinary integrator handle it. (UNVERIFIED)

A RISM model that solves the integral equations for a homogeneous fluid, giving site-to-site correlation functions that depend only on distance. It describes the structure of the bulk solvent itself, with no solute present. Its output is the required input for a 3-dimensional calculation around a solute. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical mechanical model of molecular liquids that predicts how solvent molecules arrange themselves around a solute by solving integral equations for site-to-site correlation functions. It gives an atomistic picture of solvation without simulating individual solvent molecules moving. It sits between an implicit solvent model and explicit solvent in both cost and detail. (UNVERIFIED)

A RISM model corrected so that its results reproduce the known dielectric constant of the solvent. Standard RISM does not, which distorts long-range electrostatics. The correction matters most for solvation free energies of charged solutes. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic property giving the average kinetic energy of the particles in a system, expressed on a conventional scale. In a simulation it is computed from the velocities and fluctuates strongly, because the system is small. A value quoted from a short stretch of trajectory can differ from the target by several degrees for that reason alone. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field feature in which an atom's effective size changes with the partial charge it currently carries. A real atom shrinks as it loses electron density and expands as it gains it, which a fixed radius cannot represent. It matters most for atoms whose charge varies widely between environments. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical tight binding method parameterised to give good geometries, vibrational frequencies and non-covalent interactions across most of the periodic table. It was fitted against those 3 targets rather than against energies, which is what its name records. It is used to optimise structures and screen conformations quickly. (UNVERIFIED)

A semi-empirical tight binding method that adds atom-centred multipoles and a density-dependent dispersion treatment to the earlier method in its family. Those additions improve non-covalent interactions and the description of charged systems. It is the member of the family in general use. (UNVERIFIED)

A correction applied to free energy calculations in which the electronic description changes between the 2 states, adjusting for the mismatch between them. Without it the computed difference contains a contribution from the change of method rather than from the chemistry. It is applied after the calculation rather than changing how it runs. (UNVERIFIED)

A correction applied to free energy calculations run with a particular polarizable force field, adjusting for the way that force field attenuates interactions at short range. Without it the computed free energies carry a systematic offset. It is applied after the calculation rather than changing how it runs. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field that allows bonds to form and break during a simulation, by making the bonding terms depend on how many neighbours each atom currently has rather than on a fixed list. That removes the fixed topology an ordinary force field relies on. It reaches system sizes no quantum method can while still describing reactions, at a cost far above a conventional force field. (UNVERIFIED)

A reactive force field in which the strength of every bond is recomputed from interatomic distances at each step, so bonds can form and break. Charges are also recomputed, since they change as bonds do. It reaches system sizes no quantum method can while still describing reactions, at perhaps 100 times the cost of a conventional force field. (UNVERIFIED)

An adjustment that replaces the van der Waals parameters for one particular pair of atom types, overriding whatever the combining rule would give. It exists because the combining rule is a convenience rather than physics, and fails badly for some pairs, ions with carboxylate oxygens in particular. It is applied pair by pair rather than by changing the atom types themselves. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes the induced dipole on each atom in a polarizable force field. Each induced dipole changes the field felt by the others, so they must be solved together rather than one at a time. That coupling is what makes a polarizable simulation several times more expensive than a fixed-charge one. (UNVERIFIED)

A classical model that computes induced dipoles in a set of polarizable atoms by giving each a point polarizability and solving the resulting linear equations self-consistently. It captures how the dipole induced on one atom polarizes its neighbours in turn. It diverges when atoms are too close together, which later schemes damp. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: RESP permanent virtual site charge model

definition.val: A charge model that fits point charges to the electrostatic potential while allowing some of them to sit at fixed positions away from any nucleus. Placing charge off-nucleus reproduces directional features, such as a lone pair, without the cost of higher multipole terms. It is the cheaper alternative to a multipole description. (UNVERIFIED)

A potential energy function formed as a straight-line interpolation between the functions of an initial and a final state, controlled by a coupling parameter running from 0 to 1. It is what makes a continuous path between 2 chemically different states possible in an alchemical calculation. It behaves badly when atoms appear or disappear, which is why the soft-core variant exists. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format defining, for each residue that can gain or lose a proton, the topology and charges of every protonation state it can take and the reference energy of each. A constant pH simulation reads it to know what states are available and what switching between them costs. A residue absent from the library cannot titrate. (UNVERIFIED)

A force field component that adds an energy correction read from a 2-dimensional grid indexed by a pair of neighbouring backbone rotation angles. The pair of angles is treated together rather than as 2 independent terms, which is what lets the correction fix their coupling. It was introduced to bring simulated backbone conformational populations into line with experiment. (UNVERIFIED)

A restraint potential is an artificial energy function that is added to the force field to guide a simulation. This potential adds an energy penalty when the system deviates from a user-defined geometric target, such as a specific distance, angle, or RMSD value.

A statistical mechanical theory that describes solvent around a solute by treating the solvent as a fluid whose density and orientation vary with position. It assigns energy and entropy to each region rather than to the system as a whole. That local assignment is what lets individual water sites be scored for displacement by a ligand. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation technique in which the box is treated as one cell of an infinite lattice of identical copies, so a particle leaving one side re-enters the opposite side. It removes the surface that a finite box would otherwise have, where molecules would behave unlike those in bulk. The box must be large enough that a molecule does not interact with its own image. (UNVERIFIED)

An expanded ensemble simulation is an enhanced sampling method where the simulation samples not only the coordinates of the system but also an additional thermodynamic variable, such as temperature or an alchemical coupling parameter. The system can move dynamically between different temperatures or states, which helps it to overcome energy barriers and sample a wider range of conformations. For experts, this method is a powerful framework that generalizes techniques like replica-exchange and lambda-dynamics for calculating free energies.

A software program that assembles the parts of a simulation into a system that is ready to run. It places the molecule in a box, fills the box with solvent, adds ions to reach the intended charge and concentration, and writes the topology and coordinate files. It is the step at which a structure becomes a simulatable system. (UNVERIFIED)

A system preparation program that inserts a stated number of molecules, such as solvent or ions, into a simulation box that already contains other molecules. It places them without creating overlaps. It is used at the end of system preparation to reach a target composition or density. (UNVERIFIED)

An electrostatics analysis tool is a type of software designed to calculate and visualize the electrostatic properties of a molecule. These tools typically take a molecular structure with assigned atomic charges and compute quantities like the electrostatic potential on the molecule's surface or the total electrostatic energy of solvation. They are essential for understanding how a molecule will interact with other charged molecules and its polar solvent environment.

A numerical solver that computes the electrostatic potential around a molecule in solvent by solving the Poisson-Boltzmann equation on a grid that is refined where the potential changes fastest. Refining only where needed gives the accuracy of a fine grid at much lower cost. It is the usual way continuum electrostatics is computed for a large biomolecule. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of van der Waals radii in the modified-Bondi series, with further adjustments to the radii of specific atoms including carboxylate oxygens and the hydrogens bonded to nitrogen. It was fitted for use with a particular generalized Born model and improves salt-bridge and nucleic acid behaviour. It is the third revision in that series. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program that processes the output of a constant pH molecular dynamics run and reports pKa values and titration curves for the titratable residues. It reads the record of protonation state changes rather than the trajectory. It is what turns a constant pH simulation into a number that can be compared with experiment. (UNVERIFIED)

A defined set of functions and rules through which one piece of software uses another. It fixes what can be asked for and what comes back, so the 2 sides can change independently as long as the agreement holds. It is how a simulation engine is driven from a script rather than from a command line. (UNVERIFIED)

A programming platform and interface for running general computation on NVIDIA graphics processors. A graphics processor performs thousands of simple operations at once, which suits computing forces on many atoms simultaneously. Most simulation engines run several times faster through it than on processors alone, at the cost of working only on one manufacturer's hardware. (UNVERIFIED)

A software program that computes free energy differences from the data produced by enhanced sampling simulations. It implements estimators such as the weighted histogram analysis method or the multi-state Bennett acceptance ratio, which combine data across simulation windows. It is the last step of a free energy workflow, turning many biased runs into 1 number. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program that computes free energy differences across the edges of an alchemical network using the multi-state Bennett acceptance ratio estimator. Treating the calculation as a network lets inconsistencies around closed cycles be detected and corrected. It is built for campaigns of many ligands rather than single pairs. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library is a collection of pre-written code and subroutines that provide specific functionalities to be used by other programs. Libraries are not executed directly by end-users but are imported or linked by developers to perform specialized tasks, such as mathematical computations or file parsing.

A software library for computing discrete Fourier transforms, which convert data between a description in space or time and one in frequency. Particle mesh Ewald performs one at every step, so its speed sets a large part of a simulation's cost. The library measures the machine it is running on and chooses its method accordingly. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation engine, distributed with AmberTools, used for force field parameter fitting, free energy calculations and testing new algorithms as well as for ordinary molecular dynamics. It exposes parts of the calculation that the production engines keep fixed. It is a development and method-testing tool rather than a production engine. (UNVERIFIED)

A small script that performs one well-defined supporting task inside a larger workflow, such as converting between file formats or pulling one value out of an output file. It does no science itself; it makes the pieces that do fit together. A published workflow usually depends on several, which is why they are recorded here. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that converts a structure file containing a metal ion into a format carrying explicit bonds and charges. A structure file records positions and leaves bonding implicit, which is not enough to build a metal site. It is the first step of parameterising a metal centre. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of atomic radii fitted for use with the generalized Born model of the same authors. Radii and generalized Born model are fitted together, so using 1 with a different model degrades both. It is the default radii set for that model in AMBER. (UNVERIFIED)

The ndfes software, included in the FE-ToolKit package, is used to analyze biased umbrella sampling to estimate free energy surfaces in an arbitrary number of reaction coordinate dimensions using either the variational free energy profile (vFEP), multistate Bennett acceptance ratio method (MBAR), or the highly-related weighted thermodynamic perturbation and generalized weighted thermodynamic perturbation methods.

ParmEd is a software package and Python library designed for manipulating and converting molecular topology and parameter files from various simulation packages, with a primary focus on the AMBER force field format. It allows users to programmatically modify force field parameters, change molecular connectivity, and convert between different file formats.

A system preparation program that cleans a Protein Data Bank structure file so the AMBER tools can read it. It renumbers residues, corrects atom naming, and reports problems such as missing atoms, alternate locations and unusual residues. It is run before force field parameters are assigned, because those steps fail on an unprepared file. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup program that builds a larger box by repeating a small crystallographic unit cell along chosen directions. It is needed when the original cell is smaller than the distance at which interactions are cut off, which would let a molecule interact with its own image. Repeating the cell makes the box big enough for that not to happen. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in AmberTools that scores protein structures or docked poses using a choice of scoring functions. It ranks candidate structures rather than producing one. It is used to sift the output of a docking run before any of it is simulated. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that fits atomic charges to a computed electrostatic potential, with a restraint pulling charges on buried atoms towards zero. The restraint exists because the potential outside a molecule barely constrains its interior, so an unrestrained fit gives buried charges that are large and arbitrary. It is the Python implementation of that fitting procedure. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that writes the input file for the charge fitting program, recording which charges are constrained to be equal and how strongly buried atoms are restrained. Setting those constraints by hand is the part of the procedure most easily got wrong. It performs no fitting itself. (UNVERIFIED)

Pytraj is a Python library that provides a programmable interface to the powerful trajectory analysis capabilities of the cpptraj engine from the AmberTools suite. It allows users to write Python scripts to perform a wide range of analyses, such as calculating RMSD, distances, and hydrogen bonds, directly on simulation trajectories. Pytraj enables the creation of complex, automated, and reproducible analysis workflows that integrate seamlessly with other Python data science tools.

A quantum chemistry program in AmberTools that performs semi-empirical calculations, used both on its own and as the quantum part of a hybrid simulation. It implements the NDDO-based methods and the tight binding ones. It is the engine the AmberTools charge assignment tools call. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine written from the outset to run on graphics processors rather than adapted to them. Being designed for that hardware rather than ported to it gives it a substantial speed advantage on the calculations it supports. It supports fewer methods than a general-purpose package in exchange. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library that performs Poisson-Boltzmann surface area calculations using the PyTorch framework. Running the calculation that way gives it graphics processor acceleration and automatic derivatives without either being written by hand. The derivatives are what let the solvation term contribute forces during a simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup program that rebuilds a complete crystallographic repeating unit from a structure file by applying the symmetry operations recorded in it. A deposited file usually contains only the smallest unique part, leaving the rest to be generated. The program performs that generation so the full contents of the cell can be simulated. (UNVERIFIED)

A graphical system preparation program that builds a molecular system for AMBER interactively: loading a structure, applying a force field, adding solvent and ions, and writing the topology and coordinate files. It is the graphical front end to the same engine the command-line tool uses. The 2 produce identical output from identical commands. (UNVERIFIED)

A program that turns source code into a working executable, working out what must be compiled and in what order. It also finds the libraries the program depends on and links them in. Which options it was given affects how fast the resulting program runs, and sometimes what it can do. (UNVERIFIED)

A build system tool that reads a single description of how a program is assembled and generates the build files each platform's compiler expects. It lets one set of instructions serve Linux, macOS and Windows. Most simulation software is built with it, so which version was used is part of reproducing an installation. (UNVERIFIED)

The Intel oneAPI Math Kernel Library (oneMKL) is a collection of highly optimized mathematical functions for science, engineering, and financial applications, specifically tuned for Intel processors. It provides high-performance implementations of routines for linear algebra (BLAS, LAPACK, ScaLAPACK), Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT), and other core mathematical operations. For biomolecular simulation software, linking against oneMKL can significantly boost performance by accelerating the fundamental mathematical computations underlying the simulation algorithms.

A package manager is a tool that automates the process of installing, upgrading, configuring, and removing software packages and their dependencies. It simplifies the management of the complex web of software required for scientific computing by handling the details of where to find packages and which versions are compatible. For simulation scientists, package managers like Conda are crucial for creating stable and reproducible software environments.

Miniconda is a minimal, bootstrap installer for the Conda package manager, which is widely used in the scientific computing community. It includes only the Conda package manager and Python, allowing users to create customized software environments by installing only the packages they need. For researchers, Miniconda provides a lightweight way to set up isolated and reproducible environments for their simulation and analysis software.

A utility script distributed with AmberTools that fetches and applies official updates and fixes to an existing installation. It contacts the update server, downloads what applies to the installed version, and patches the source. Which updates have been applied is part of what identifies the version a result came from. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program that solves the 1-dimensional RISM equations for a pure solvent, giving its structural and thermodynamic properties. Its output describes the bulk liquid with no solute present. It must be run before any 3-dimensional RISM calculation, which takes those results as input. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine for density functional theory written to run on graphics processors. Its integral evaluation is the part moved onto that hardware, which is where most of the time in such a calculation goes. It is used as the quantum part of hybrid simulations, where the same calculation must be repeated at every step. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry program for very high accuracy electronic structure calculations, implementing coupled cluster methods to arbitrary excitation level and their multi-reference forms. Those methods are the benchmark other methods are measured against. Its cost restricts it to small systems. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine that performs density functional calculations using orbitals confined to a fixed radius around each atom, with the resulting integrals tabulated in advance. Confining the orbitals is what makes the tabulation possible and the calculation fast. It is used for large systems where full density functional theory would be too slow. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine implementing density functional tight binding, an approximation that replaces most of the electronic integrals with values tabulated in advance. It is 2 to 3 orders of magnitude faster than full density functional theory while remaining quantum mechanical. Its accuracy depends on parameters fitted for each pair of elements, so it works only for element combinations that have been parameterised. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry program implementing the extended tight binding family of semi-empirical methods. It is fast enough to optimise geometries and search conformations for molecules of a few hundred atoms in seconds. It is widely used as a preliminary step before a more expensive calculation. (UNVERIFIED)

A software framework that connects separate simulation programs so that each can compute the part of a system it is best suited to. It passes coordinates, energies and forces between them and keeps them in step. It is what allows a quantum chemistry program and a molecular dynamics program to run 1 simulation together. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library that lets a classical simulation program request energies and forces from the TeraChem quantum chemistry program over a network connection. The 2 programs run separately and exchange data at each step. It is what allows a quantum and a classical engine to run one hybrid simulation together. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation engine built to run reactive force field simulations, where bonding is recomputed at every step rather than fixed. Recomputing the bond network is what makes such a simulation expensive, and the engine is written around doing it in parallel. It is used for reactions in materials and at surfaces. (UNVERIFIED)

A structure preparation program that adds hydrogen atoms to a macromolecular structure and chooses their positions. It also decides how to orient groups whose 2 possible arrangements X-ray data cannot distinguish, such as the ends of asparagine and glutamine side chains. Crystallography rarely sees hydrogens, so a structure file usually arrives without them and a simulation cannot start until they are there. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup utility that places the hydrogen atoms of water molecules taken from an experimental structure. Crystallography sees the oxygen of an ordered water and not its hydrogens, so their orientation must be worked out. It chooses orientations that make sensible hydrogen bonds with the surroundings. (UNVERIFIED)

Pdbremix is a utility designed for advanced manipulation and modification of Protein Data Bank (PDB) files. It allows users to perform a wide range of tasks such as renumbering residues, changing atom or residue names, and translating or rotating parts of a molecule. Experts use this tool for complex system-building tasks that require precise, custom modifications to a standard PDB file before simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

A system preparation program that builds an initial arrangement of molecules inside a defined region by packing them to satisfy stated counts and spatial constraints while keeping them from overlapping. It solves a constrained optimisation rather than placing molecules at random. It is how a mixed or layered starting system is built when a regular lattice will not do. (UNVERIFIED)

AMBAT is a software tool used to construct three-dimensional models of cell membranes for use in AMBER molecular simulations. Consisting of a set of scripts, it automates the complex process of arranging lipid molecules to form a proper bilayer and can then embed a protein structure within that prepared membrane. As part of the AmberTools suite, AMBAT (Amber Membrane Builder and Analysis Tool) provides a script-based workflow for both the initial construction of lipid bilayer systems and for subsequent analysis of membrane properties, serving as a specialized tool for preparing membrane protein simulations.

synonyms.val: Amber Membrane Builder and Analysis Tool

definition.val: A software program that derives force field parameters by adjusting them until the force field reproduces reference data, usually quantum calculations. It is used when no existing parameter covers a molecule and assignment by analogy is not good enough. Its output is a parameter set, not a prepared system. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program that searches automatically for force field parameters giving the best agreement with reference data, by trying many combinations rather than fitting one term at a time. Searching the whole space at once can find a combination that fitting terms separately misses. It is used for parameter development rather than for preparing a single system. (UNVERIFIED)

comments: described in https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.1079

definition.val: A utility program in AmberTools that checks whether every parameter a molecule needs is present in the chosen force field, and writes an additional parameter file supplying the missing ones by analogy. Missing parameters otherwise stop system preparation with an error. Parameters it supplies by analogy are guesses and are flagged as such in its output. (UNVERIFIED)

An interactive utility included in the AmberTools software package for deriving force field parameters. It assists users in calculating new parameters for bond lengths and angles based on a set of built-in empirical rules. This tool is particularly useful when parameterizing a new molecule for which no existing force field parameters are available. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that fits rotation parameters by adjusting them until the force field reproduces energies computed quantum mechanically along a rotation. Rotation terms are the ones most often wrong for a new molecule, because they depend on the whole local environment. It is used when the parameters supplied by analogy are not good enough. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that builds force field parameters for a metal centre in a protein, from quantum calculations on the metal and the groups around it. A metal site has no standard parameters, because its geometry and charge depend on which groups coordinate it. It automates a procedure that is otherwise long and easy to get wrong. (UNVERIFIED)

A Python toolkit for parameterising metal sites in biomolecules, providing the components that the metal centre parameter builder is assembled from. It handles the quantum calculations, the charge fitting and the assembly of the resulting parameters. It is a toolkit rather than a single program. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that assigns a force field atom type to every atom of a molecule, from its element and its bonding environment. Every parameter a molecule receives follows from those assignments. It is run before parameters are looked up, and its output is worth inspecting for unusual chemistry. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that assigns partial charges to an organic molecule by running a fast semi-empirical calculation and then applying tabulated corrections based on each bond's type. The corrections are fitted so the result approximates a far more expensive fitted charge set. It is how charges are produced for a ligand in seconds rather than hours. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that works out the bond order of each bond in a molecule, distinguishing single, double and aromatic bonds. Structure files often record coordinates without bond orders, which must then be inferred from geometry. The result determines which parameters the bond receives. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that writes the input files for a restrained fit of atomic charges to a computed electrostatic potential. It sets up which charges are constrained to be equal and how strongly buried atoms are restrained, which is the part that is easy to get wrong by hand. The fit itself is performed by a separate program. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that builds a residue template file for a new molecule from its structure and charges. It works out the connection tree and which atoms serve as the head and tail. It is run once per new building block, and its output is reused thereafter. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility program in AmberTools that produces a complete residue template for a new molecule, running charge assignment and atom typing and then building the template. It automates the sequence of steps that the individual tools would otherwise be run through by hand. It is the usual route for adding a modified residue. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantum chemistry engine that divides a large molecule into overlapping regions, solves each separately, and assembles the result. Doing so makes the cost grow in proportion to the system size rather than far faster, which is what puts whole proteins within reach. The overlap between regions is what keeps the joins from introducing errors. (UNVERIFIED)

A validation script that inspects a small molecule structure file for the faults that stop force field parameters being assigned, such as wrong atom types, bad connectivity and inconsistent valences. It reports each fault and in some cases corrects it. It is run before antechamber rather than after a failure. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script in AmberTools that helps fit parameters for ion models, by running simulations at trial parameter values and comparing the resulting hydration free energies and ion-water distances against measurements. Ion parameters must be fitted against such properties rather than derived, because no calculation gives them directly. It automates the repeated trials that fitting requires. (UNVERIFIED)

This is a utility script designed to search for and retrieve specific molecular structure files from the Protein Data Bank (PDB). It allows a user to programmatically find structures based on criteria such as the PDB ID, the name of the molecule, or the experimental method used. This automates the process of gathering the necessary input structures for a large-scale simulation or analysis project. (UNVERIFIED)

A system preparation script that writes 1 input file per replica for a replica exchange molecular dynamics run, from a template and a list of temperatures. A replica exchange run needs as many input files as it has replicas, which is too many to write by hand. It is what makes the number of replicas a parameter rather than a chore. (UNVERIFIED)

The nfe-umbrella-slice script is a utility used in the analysis of umbrella sampling simulations, likely as part of a larger free energy calculation workflow. Its purpose is to extract a specific portion or "slice" of the simulation data from the collective output of all umbrella windows. Experts use this for tasks such as assessing the convergence of the free energy profile by analyzing how it changes as more data is included.

A system preparation script, part of AmberTools, that writes the input file a constant pH molecular dynamics run needs. It records which residues may change protonation state and the parameters the titration algorithm uses. Without it the simulation has no list of titratable sites. (UNVERIFIED)

The ceinutil.py script is a utility used to prepare the input files for constant redox-potential MD simulations in AMBER. It allows the user to specify which residues can change their redox state and defines the parameters for the simulation. This script is essential for setting up simulations that model the behavior of molecules in a specific electrochemical environment.

A system preparation script that writes the input file for a simulation holding both pH and redox potential constant. It records which residues may change protonation state and which may change oxidation state. It is the constant pH preparation script extended to redox-active sites. (UNVERIFIED)

The cyana_rest_to_amberRST script iscript converts CYANA .upl upper distance limit files into AMBER .RST format, allowing for the inclusion of restraints in molecular dynamics simulations. This conversion tool is commonly used to prepare input data for AMBER's sander or pmemd applications.

This script is a utility for creating a restraint file (RST) for a simulation that uses direct dipolar coupling (DIP) data from NMR experiments. It likely reads experimental dipolar coupling values and generates the corresponding energy restraint terms in a format that can be read by a simulation program like AMBER. This automates the process of incorporating this specific type of experimental data into a simulation.

placeAV.py is a utility script used to convert the predicted solvent binding sites from a Placevent analysis into explicit atomic coordinates. It reads the centers of high-density solvent regions determined by the analysis and places dummy atoms or water molecules at those specific locations within a structure file. This tool allows researchers to visualize potential hydration sites or use them as defined starting positions for explicit solvent molecules in subsequent simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

The FRETrest.py script is a utility used to generate distance restraints for a molecular dynamics simulation based on experimental data from Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) experiments. It translates the efficiency of energy transfer between two fluorescent labels into a distance distribution that can be used to bias the simulation.

The ambpdb utility is a command-line tool in the AmberTools suite that converts AMBER's native topology (.prmtop) and coordinate (.inpcrd or .rst7) files into the standard Protein Data Bank (PDB) format.

A system preparation script that derives the separate receptor and ligand topology files needed for an end-point binding free energy calculation by stripping atoms from the topology of the complex. Deriving them this way guarantees the 3 topologies are consistent. Building them independently is the common source of mismatched-topology errors. (UNVERIFIED)

A Perl script used as part of the FEW (Free Energy Workflow) software to post-process simulation data. Its primary function is to parse output files and calculate a summary of effective binding energies from a free energy calculation. This script automates the data extraction step, making the analysis of complex binding energy simulations more efficient. (UNVERIFIED)

The extract_LIEenergies.pl script is a utility designed to parse simulation output files and extract the specific energy components required for a Linear Interaction Energy (LIE) calculation. It typically reads the log files to find the average van der Waals and electrostatic interaction energies of a ligand with its environment. For researchers using the LIE method, this script automates the data extraction step needed to calculate the binding free energy. (UNVERIFIED)

This script is a utility used in the setup of alchemical free energy calculations to automatically identify the atoms that change between two different ligand structures. It likely compares two molecule files and generates a list of the atoms that are unique to each, which is necessary for defining the alchemical transformation. This automates a key and often error-prone step in preparing relative binding free energy calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

The bar_pbsa.py script is a utility that likely combines results from Bennett Acceptance Ratio (BAR) free energy calculations with endpoint MM/PBSA calculations. This hybrid approach may be used to refine free energy estimates or to decompose a rigorously calculated free energy into physically intuitive components. For experts in free energy methods, this script represents a tool for advanced, multi-step analysis workflows. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that converts output files from AMBER simulations into the specific data format required by the edgembar free energy analysis program. It processes AMBER's energy or log files to extract the necessary potential energy values for each frame of the simulation. This script is an essential data preparation step for using the edgembar tool to analyze free energy calculations that were performed with the AMBER software. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script from the edgembar software package that visualizes the results of a large-scale free energy calculation. It takes the calculated free energy differences between many different molecules and generates an interactive HTML file that displays the results as a network graph. This allows researchers to easily explore the relationships and predicted binding affinities for a whole series of compounds in a web browser. (UNVERIFIED)

This is a utility script from the edgembar software package used to process the output from a specific type of free energy calculation. It likely extracts the necessary energy data from simulations of the "bookend" or reference states in a large alchemical network. This data preparation is a required step before the main edgembar program can combine all the results to calculate the final relative free energies. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that generates the list of coupling parameter values a thermodynamic integration calculation will simulate, choosing their number and spacing. Even spacing is wasteful, because the integrand changes much faster near the end points than in the middle. It produces the schedule before the simulations are run rather than adjusting it during them. (UNVERIFIED)

This script is a utility designed to convert simulation output files from the AMBER software package into a format that can be used by the ndfes free energy analysis toolkit. It reads AMBER trajectory and output files and extracts the necessary data, such as the values of collective variables over time. This is an essential interoperability step for analyzing AMBER simulations with the ndfes suite of tools. (UNVERIFIED)

This script is a utility used to check if a simulation has reached a stable equilibrium. It analyzes a time-series of a specific property, such as a collective variable, from a simulation output file to determine if its average value has stopped fluctuating systematically. This is a crucial step in free energy calculations to ensure that the data used for analysis is from a well-equilibrated system. (UNVERIFIED)

This script is a utility for combining multiple metadata files generated during a free energy calculation, particularly from metadynamics simulations. It merges the information about the biasing potential that was added at different times or from different parallel runs into a single, unified file. This is a necessary data processing step before the final free energy surface can be reconstructed from the combined simulation data. (UNVERIFIED)

This script is a utility that takes the final, processed data from a free energy calculation and writes it out as a human-readable file representing the free energy surface (FES). The output is typically a data grid where each point has a coordinate and a corresponding free energy value. This file is the final result of the calculation and is used directly for plotting and visualizing the energetic landscape of the molecular process. (UNVERIFIED)

This script is a utility from a specific software package (ndfes) used to average multiple free energy surfaces (FESs). It likely takes several free energy profiles, for example from replicate simulations, and calculates their average and standard deviation. This is a standard final step in free energy analysis to obtain a statistically robust result and estimate its uncertainty. (UNVERIFIED)

This is a computational tool used to find the most likely transition pathway between two stable molecular shapes on a free energy surface. It takes a pre-calculated free energy landscape and uses an algorithm to identify the minimum free energy path connecting two specified states. This analysis is used to understand the mechanism and sequence of events during a conformational change or a chemical reaction. (UNVERIFIED)

This script is a utility used to create a plausible starting guess for the transition pathway between two molecular conformations. It typically generates a series of intermediate structures by linearly interpolating between the known start and end states. This initial guess provides a starting point for more sophisticated path-finding algorithms that then refine the path to find the minimum free energy route. (UNVERIFIED)

This script is a utility for analyzing the set of simulations that were run to determine a transition pathway. It processes the trajectories from simulations performed along a path to refine its position or to calculate properties, such as the average force, along that path. This analysis is a key part of iterative path-finding methods that use simulation data to converge on the minimum free energy path. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that selects a reference free energy value from a set of calculations, so that every result in the set can be quoted relative to the same zero point. A relative free energy calculation gives differences, not absolute values, so a common reference has to be chosen before results can be compared. It reads the calculation outputs and reports which value it chose. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that extracts the electrostatic potential and the points it was computed at from quantum chemistry output, and writes them in the form a charge fitting program expects. It is a format conversion between 2 steps of charge derivation. It performs no fitting itself. (UNVERIFIED)

A utility script that runs the whole charge derivation procedure end to end: the quantum calculation, the extraction of the potential, the construction of the fitting input and the fit itself. Doing it in one step removes the several file conversions the separate tools require. Those conversions are where the procedure is usually got wrong. (UNVERIFIED)

The chamber script is a utility within the AmberTools suite that facilitates the conversion of CHARMM-formatted force field files into a format that can be used by AMBER. It processes CHARMM topology (PSF) and parameter (PAR) files, allowing users to run simulations with CHARMM force fields using the AMBER simulation engines.

match_atomname is a utility program within the AmberTools suite that takes an input file and a reference file in pdb, ac, prepi, prepc and mol2 format and it automatically detects the corresponding atom name in the reference for each atom name in the input. An output file in the same format as that of the input is generated using the matched atom names. Designed to recover atom-name information lost after running Gaussian calculations.

A software library implementing the message passing standard, providing the functions a parallel program calls to send and receive data between machines. The standard says what the functions do; a library is a working version of them. Which one is installed affects performance but not results. (UNVERIFIED)

An implementation of the message passing standard that moves data directly between graphics processors on different machines, without routing it through their central processors. Avoiding that detour removes a large part of the delay in a simulation running across several machines with accelerators. It requires network hardware that supports direct access. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library for finding a few eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a very large matrix without forming the whole matrix. Normal mode analysis of a large structure needs exactly that, since only the slowest modes are of interest. Computing every mode would be impossible for a system of that size. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational tool used to predict the acidity constant, or pKa, of ionizable groups in a protein or other molecule. It takes a 3D structure as input and uses a model, often based on continuum electrostatics, to calculate how the local chemical environment shifts the pKa of each titratable residue. This is a critical preparation step for any simulation, as it allows for the assignment of the correct protonation states for all residues at a given experimental pH. (UNVERIFIED)

A system preparation program that rewrites a topology file to contain several non-interacting copies of a chosen region of a molecule, as locally enhanced sampling requires. The copies feel the rest of the system but not each other. It is run before the simulation, because the method cannot be switched on afterwards. (UNVERIFIED)

A formal system of instructions and syntax rules in which computer programs are written. Which one a tool is written in affects how fast it runs and how easily it can be changed or extended. It is recorded because reproducing a computational result may require the same language version. (UNVERIFIED)

NAB, or Nucleic Acid Builder, is a specialized programming language designed specifically for the purpose of constructing and manipulating three-dimensional models of nucleic acids and proteins. For experts, NAB provides a powerful and scriptable way to build complex or non-standard biomolecular structures that would be difficult to create with standard graphical tools. Originally distributed with the AmberTools software suite, it is now only available from an independent GitHub repository.
The FE-ToolKit is a collection of tools designed to facilitate the setup, execution, and analysis of alchemical free energy simulations and umbrella sampling.

An analysis program that computes a theoretical small-angle X-ray scattering profile from a structure together with a solvent distribution from 3D-RISM theory. Including the ordered solvent layer matters because that layer scatters measurably. It differs from the trajectory-based tool in obtaining the solvent from theory rather than from sampling. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis program that computes a theoretical small-angle X-ray scattering profile from a molecular dynamics trajectory, by averaging the scattering of the sampled conformations. Averaging over an ensemble is what makes the result comparable with a measurement on a solution. It uses the trajectory alone, with no explicit solvent model. (UNVERIFIED)

A collection of separate programs distributed and installed together, sharing file formats and conventions so that the output of one is directly usable by the next. AmberTools and GROMACS are examples. The distinction from a single program matters, because a suite's name is often used loosely for the one program in it that a study actually ran. (UNVERIFIED)

A software suite for developing, fitting and checking force field parameters. It covers the whole process from quantum calculations through fitting to validation against reference data. It is used to build a parameter set rather than to prepare a single system. (UNVERIFIED)

Metatwist is an analysis tool for studying the twisting motions of helical molecules, such as DNA, using data from a metadynamics simulation. It is probably designed to analyze a free energy surface calculated as a function of a helical twist collective variable. This would allow a researcher to quantify the energetic cost and identify the pathways associated with the twisting and untwisting of a molecular helix. (UNVERIFIED)

A trajectory analysis program, formerly part of the AMBER suite, that read a script of commands and computed properties such as RMSD, distances and angles from a coordinate file. It has been superseded by cpptraj, which is faster and handles more formats. It is retained because older published workflows refer to it. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that converts a continuous solvent density map into a list of discrete water positions, by repeatedly taking the highest remaining peak and removing the density around it. A simulation needs individual water molecules, and a theory-derived map gives only a density. It is the step that turns one into the other. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation engine, distributed with the commercial AMBER package, optimised for speed on large systems and on graphics processing units. It supports fewer methods than the general-purpose engine but runs the common ones far faster. It is the engine most production molecular dynamics in AMBER is run with. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation engine, distributed with AmberTools, that performs energy minimisation, molecular dynamics and some free energy calculations. It is the general-purpose engine of the suite and supports the widest range of methods. It is slower than the optimised engine in the commercial package, which is the trade for that breadth. (UNVERIFIED)

A software service reached through a web browser that runs a computational tool on the user's behalf and returns the result. Nothing is installed locally, which puts methods within reach of people who could not otherwise run them. The trade is that the input leaves the user's machine and the version that ran it cannot be pinned down later. (UNVERIFIED)

GLYCAM-Web is a collection of online tools and web servers that assist researchers in building three-dimensional models of carbohydrates and glycoproteins. It uses the GLYCAM force field to generate realistic structures and provides tools for tasks like predicting the conformation of glycosidic linkages.

The Glycoprotein Builder is a web-based tool that automates the process of constructing three-dimensional models of glycoproteins. It allows users to start with a protein structure and graphically attach various glycan (sugar chain) structures to specific amino acid residues. For researchers, this tool greatly simplifies the otherwise complex and tedious task of building a complete, simulation-ready model of a glycosylated protein.

An open-source software library for working with chemical structures, covering reading and writing file formats, computing molecular descriptors, generating 3-dimensional conformations and comparing molecules. It is the foundation most cheminformatics workflows in Python are built on. It handles the chemistry around a simulation rather than the simulation itself. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library for running molecular dynamics, designed to be called from a program rather than run as a command. It is built around graphics processors and is among the fastest engines available on them. Being a library rather than an application is what makes it the usual foundation for new methods. (UNVERIFIED)

A standard specifying how parts of a parallel program running on separate machines exchange data by sending messages to one another. Because the machines share no memory, every piece of shared information must be sent explicitly. It is how a single simulation is spread across the nodes of a cluster. (UNVERIFIED)

A programming interface that lets parts of a program run on several processor cores that share the same memory, by marking sections of the code rather than rewriting it. It is how most simulation engines use the cores of a single machine. It does not spread work across separate machines, which needs a different mechanism. (UNVERIFIED)

A specification of low-level linear algebra routines, such as multiplying a matrix by a vector or by another matrix. Hardware vendors supply versions tuned for their own processors, so the same program runs at very different speeds depending on which is installed. Almost every numerical library is built on top of it. (UNVERIFIED)

A software library providing routines for linear algebra problems such as solving systems of equations, finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and least-squares fitting. Normal mode analysis, principal component analysis and many other analyses reduce to calls into it. Its speed determines how large a matrix those analyses can handle. (UNVERIFIED)

DL-Find is a software library that provides a collection of robust algorithms for geometry optimization tasks. It contains routines for efficiently finding energy minima (stable structures) and first-order saddle points (transition states) on a potential energy surface. This library acts as an optimization engine that can be incorporated into other simulation or quantum chemistry programs to perform complex structural searches and reaction path calculations.

A software library that reads force field definition files and makes their parameters available to a program. It handles the file formats the parameters are distributed in, so that each simulation program does not need its own reader. It is a component used inside other software rather than a program a user runs. (UNVERIFIED)

x3DNA is a comprehensive software package for the analysis, rebuilding, and visualization of three-dimensional nucleic acid structures. It takes a DNA or RNA structure file as input and calculates a wide range of standard helical and base pair parameters that are used to describe the detailed geometry of the helix. It is a cornerstone tool in the field of nucleic acid structural biology for characterizing and comparing experimental or simulated structures.

A simulation engine that computes intermolecular interactions by summing separately fitted contributions from pairs, triples and larger groups of molecules. Building up the interaction this way reaches near quantum accuracy for water and small molecules. Its cost rises steeply with the size of the groups included. (UNVERIFIED)

A match analysis tool is a program that compares two or more molecular structures or datasets to find and quantify their similarities. This can involve superimposing two protein structures to calculate their RMSD or searching a database of small molecules to find ones that have a similar shape or chemical features to a query compound.

An integration algorithm that advances a simulation using a weighted average of momenta from more than one point in the step. The averaging damps the numerical error that accumulates in a plain scheme. It is intended to permit a longer timestep than the standard integrators allow. (UNVERIFIED)

A software framework that automates a binding free energy calculation by the linear interaction energy method, running the simulations of the bound and free ligand and combining their averaged interaction energies. It carries out in 1 step what would otherwise be a hand-assembled sequence of runs. The empirical coefficients it applies are what turn the energy differences into a free energy. (UNVERIFIED)

A software framework that automates a relative binding free energy calculation by thermodynamic integration, preparing the system, running the series of coupling states and analysing the result. It removes the bookkeeping of managing many simultaneous runs. It is the thermodynamic integration counterpart to the linear interaction energy workflow. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical solver is an algorithm that finds approximate solutions to complex mathematical equations that cannot be solved by hand. These algorithms are the computational engines that solve the underlying mathematical problems in many scientific simulations. For experts, this includes iterative algorithms like the conjugate gradient method used to solve the large systems of linear equations that arise in implicit solvent models or quantum mechanical calculations. (UNVERIFIED)

An iterative algorithm for solving a large system of linear equations whose matrix is not symmetric. The ordinary conjugate gradient method requires symmetry and fails without it. It is used for the equations arising in continuum electrostatics, where the matrix is not symmetric. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: modified direct inversion in the iterative subspace solver algorithm

definition.val: An algorithm that speeds up an iterative calculation by combining several previous iterations into a better next guess, with the combination chosen to make the estimated error smallest. It is the standard way a self-consistent field calculation is brought to convergence. Without it many calculations oscillate indefinitely instead of settling. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that advances the positions and velocities of the atoms from one step to the next, using the forces computed at the current step. It approximates the continuous equations of motion by a sequence of small jumps. How well it conserves energy over a long run is the main thing that separates one from another. (UNVERIFIED)
