An integration algorithm that advances positions and velocities using the forces at the current and 2 previous steps. It produces the same trajectory as the Verlet family but computes velocities more accurately at each point. That matters when a quantity depending on velocity, such as kinetic energy, is being reported. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: modified incomplete Choleski conjugate gradient solver algorithm

definition.val: An iterative algorithm for solving a large system of linear equations that first computes a rough approximate factorisation of the matrix and uses it to make the problem easier to solve. The approximation is deliberately incomplete, because an exact one would cost as much as solving the system directly. It converges in far fewer iterations than the unaided method. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes the approximate value of a definite integral from values sampled at discrete points. It is used wherever the function being integrated is known only at the points where it was measured or computed. The free energy of a thermodynamic integration calculation is obtained this way. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical integration algorithm for integrating a function over the surface of a sphere, using a fixed set of points and weights chosen to be exact for spherical harmonics up to a given order. It reaches a given accuracy with far fewer points than an evenly spaced arrangement. It supplies the angular part of the grid used in density functional theory. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes a property or finds a pattern in raw simulation data. It is the concrete procedure an analysis method is carried out by, as distinct from the idea of the method itself. Two programs implementing the same method can use different algorithms and give slightly different numbers. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis algorithm that examines or transforms data recorded as a sequence in time. A trajectory is such a sequence, so techniques built for signals apply to it directly. Smoothing, filtering and decomposing a series into its frequencies all belong here. (UNVERIFIED)

A signal processing algorithm that removes frequencies above or below a chosen point while leaving the remaining ones as flat as possible. Flatness in the kept range is what it optimises, at the cost of a gradual rather than sharp cut-off. It is used to separate slow collective motion in a trajectory from fast thermal noise. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical integration algorithm that approximates the area under a curve by joining neighbouring points with straight lines and summing the resulting trapezoids. It needs only the sampled points, with no assumption about the function between them. It is the usual way the thermodynamic integration curve is integrated over the coupling parameter. (UNVERIFIED)

A random number generator is an algorithm designed to produce a sequence of numbers that lacks any discernible pattern, appearing to be random. In computational science, these are essential for introducing the element of chance required by certain simulation methods. For experts, these pseudo-random number generators are critical components of stochastic thermostats and Monte Carlo algorithms. (UNVERIFIED)

A pseudo-random number generator of the family developed by Marsaglia, built from simple shift and multiply operations on a small internal state. The simplicity makes them fast and easy to implement, which is why they appear inside simulation engines. They pass standard statistical tests while using far less state than a long-period generator. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: Mersenne Twister random number generator algorithm

definition.val: A pseudo-random number generator that produces a sequence repeating only after an extremely long period, with no detectable pattern in ordinary statistical tests. It is the default generator in many scientific libraries. It is not suitable where an adversary must not predict the sequence, which does not arise in simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: permuted congruential random number generator algorithm

definition.val: A permuted congruential generator is a type of pseudo-random number generator that aims to improve the statistical properties of simpler linear congruential generators. It takes the output of a standard congruential generator and applies a permutation (shuffling) to its bits to break up correlations. For experts, this represents a class of generators that offers a good trade-off between computational simplicity and improved statistical quality. (UNVERIFIED)

A pseudo-random number generator built from shift, rotate and add operations on 128 bits of state. It is fast and passes current statistical test suites, and its small state makes it cheap to keep one per thread. Giving each thread its own generator is what keeps a parallel simulation reproducible. (UNVERIFIED)

MDposit is a web-based platform and portal designed for the sharing, visualization, and analysis of molecular dynamics simulation data. It serves as a distributed database interface that allows users to browse, access, and interactively view trajectories from different research groups. This tool aims to facilitate the dissemination and reuse of large-scale simulation datasets within the scientific community.

An algorithm that converts data between a description in time or space and one in frequency, in a time that grows only slightly faster than the amount of data. Computing the same transform directly would cost far more, growing with the square of the data size. It is what makes particle mesh Ewald affordable, since one is performed at every step. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering algorithm that grows a group outward from any point with enough neighbours within a chosen distance, and leaves sparse points unassigned. It needs no target number of groups and can find groups of any shape. Structures left unassigned are treated as rare conformations rather than forced into a group, which suits a trajectory well. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering algorithm that divides structures into a fixed number of groups by repeatedly assigning each to the nearest group centre and then recomputing the centres. The number of groups must be chosen in advance, which is its main limitation. It also assumes groups are roughly round and of similar size, which conformations often are not. (UNVERIFIED)

A clustering algorithm that picks group centres as points which have many close neighbours and are also far from any point with still more neighbours. Those 2 conditions identify a peak in the crowding rather than an arbitrary starting point. Every other point then joins the nearest denser point, which assigns the whole set in one pass. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm for fitting a non-linear model to data, which shifts between 2 strategies according to how well the fit is going: a cautious one far from the answer and a fast one near it. That shift is what makes it converge reliably from a poor starting guess. It is the standard method for fitting force field parameters to reference data. (UNVERIFIED)

A data file holding the complete definition of a molecular building block, giving its atoms, their types and charges, the bonds between them and their standard geometry. It lets a topology be assembled from a sequence without every atom being specified. A residue absent from it cannot be built automatically. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm that keeps a set of trial points forming a simple shape and repeatedly replaces its worst point by reflecting it through the others. It never needs a derivative, only the ability to evaluate the function. That makes it usable where derivatives are unavailable or unreliable, at the cost of converging slowly. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of effective atomic radii fitted for use with the SMx family of implicit solvent models. The radii absorb part of the error of the underlying model, which is why they are specific to it. Substituting a general-purpose set such as Bondi changes the computed solvation energies. (UNVERIFIED)

A numerical integration algorithm that evaluates a function at specially chosen points, with matching weights, so the result is exact for polynomials up to a given degree. Choosing the positions as well as the weights doubles the degree that a given number of points can handle. It needs the function to be evaluable anywhere, not only at points already sampled. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes how much of a molecule's surface a solvent molecule can reach. It does so by rolling a sphere the size of a solvent molecule over the atoms and measuring the area traced out. The result is used to estimate how much it costs to make a hole in the solvent for the molecule to sit in. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that estimates solvent-accessible surface area from a sum over overlapping pairs of atoms, with fitted coefficients, rather than by placing test points. Having a closed form makes it fast enough to run at every step of a simulation, and to be differentiated so it contributes forces. Point-based methods are more accurate and cannot do either. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that measures how far 2 structures differ, by first superposing them to remove any overall shift or rotation and then taking the root mean square of the remaining distances between matched atoms. Without the superposition step, moving a molecule across the box would register as a large change in shape. The choice of which atoms to superpose on decides what the number means. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that finds the optimal superposing rotation by solving a 4-by-4 eigenvalue problem rather than by decomposing a matrix. Representing the rotation with 4 numbers avoids the numerical failure that matrix methods can suffer when the 2 structures are nearly mirror images. It gives the same answer as the matrix route and is more robust. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm that builds an approximation to the curvature of a function from the slopes seen at successive steps, and uses it to choose each new step. Approximating the curvature rather than computing it converges in far fewer steps than using slope alone, without the cost of second derivatives. It stores a full matrix, which limits it to problems with a moderate number of variables. (UNVERIFIED)

A minimization algorithm that chooses each step from the current downhill direction combined with the previous step's direction, so that it does not undo progress already made. That memory is what lets it follow a long narrow valley, where steepest descent zig-zags. It is the usual choice once the worst overlaps in a structure have been removed. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm that finds a minimum by searching along one direction at a time and gradually replacing those directions with better ones built from the progress made. It never needs a derivative, only function values. It suits problems where derivatives are unavailable or too noisy to trust. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration algorithm that updates different forces at different intervals, evaluating the fast-changing bonded forces every step and the slow-changing long-range forces only every few steps. Most of the cost of a simulation is in the long-range forces, so evaluating them less often is a large saving. Stretching the interval too far makes the simulation unstable. (UNVERIFIED)

A multiple time-stepping algorithm that separates forces by how fast they change and nests their updates inside one another, in a way that can be run backwards to recover the starting state exactly. That reversibility is what keeps energy from drifting, which simpler multiple time-stepping schemes do not manage. It is the standard implementation of the idea. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes long-range forces quickly by grouping distant particles into a hierarchy of cells and treating each distant group as a single source. A group far enough away is indistinguishable from a point, so computing its members separately is wasted work. It reduces the cost from growing with the square of the particle count to growing close to linearly. (UNVERIFIED)

An advanced algorithm for updating atom positions in a molecular dynamics simulation that uses information from previous steps to predict the future motion. It works by extrapolating both the forces and the coordinates to the next time point, which can allow for a larger time step while maintaining numerical stability. This type of integrator is a specialized method aimed at improving the computational efficiency of a simulation. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that decides, during a simulation, which atoms belong in the quantum region at each moment. It is needed when molecules such as solvent move in and out of the region of interest, so a fixed list would either trap them or cut them in half. The difficulty is changing the assignment without a jump in energy. (UNVERIFIED)

A region selection algorithm that uses 2 distance thresholds, a nearer one for entering the quantum region and a farther one for leaving it. The gap between them stops an atom sitting exactly at the boundary from switching back and forth every step. That repeated switching is what makes a single-threshold rule unusable. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that solves the equations of quantum mechanics for a molecular system, to obtain how its electrons are arranged and what energy that costs. All such algorithms are approximate, because the exact equations cannot be solved for more than one electron. They differ in which approximation they make and what it costs. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that makes a quantum calculation on a large molecule possible by splitting it into overlapping pieces, solving each, and recombining them. A conventional calculation costs far more than proportionally more as the system grows, which is what this avoids. The pieces must overlap, or the joins between them introduce errors. (UNVERIFIED)

A multiple time-stepping algorithm of the RESPA family adapted for polarizable force fields, where the induced dipoles must be resolved at each evaluation of the long-range forces. Polarizable models make the long-range part far more expensive, so separating it out matters more than usual. It splits the forces by range as well as by how quickly they change. (UNVERIFIED)

A temperature control algorithm that couples the system to a bath variable, that variable to a second, and so on along a chain. The chain fixes a failure of the single-variable form, which cannot reach the correct distribution for a system with few degrees of freedom or one starting far from equilibrium. A chain of 3 to 5 is usual. (UNVERIFIED)

A temperature control algorithm that rescales the velocities towards the target temperature by a factor drawn partly at random, so that the energy follows the correct distribution rather than being driven to a single value. It reaches equilibrium as quickly as the simple rescaling schemes while sampling correctly, which they do not. stochastic velocity rescaling thermostat should be kept as an exact synonym. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration algorithm of the velocity-Verlet family in which the thermostat acts halfway through each step rather than at its start or end. Placing it there keeps the sampled distribution closer to the correct one when the timestep is large. The difference shows up as an error in temperature that grows with timestep in the other arrangements. (UNVERIFIED)

A polarization algorithm that gives each induced dipole a small fictitious mass and lets it move under its own equation of motion, instead of solving for it exactly at every step. If the mass is small enough the dipoles stay close to the exact solution while never being solved for. It removes the iteration that otherwise dominates the cost. (UNVERIFIED)

A way of placing the thermostat's action halfway through each integration step rather than at its beginning or end. That placement keeps the sampled distribution correct at much larger timesteps than the alternatives allow. The difference appears as a temperature error that grows with timestep in the other arrangements. (UNVERIFIED)

A set of atomic radii fitted for use with the GB-Neck2 implicit solvent model. Fitting them alongside that model is what lets it reproduce Poisson-Boltzmann solvation energies closely. They are not interchangeable with radii fitted for other generalized Born models. (UNVERIFIED)

A minimization algorithm that chooses each search direction from the current downhill slope combined with the previous direction, using a particular formula for how much of the previous one to keep. That formula is what separates it from the other conjugate gradient variants. It recovers well when progress stalls, because its formula resets the direction automatically in that case. (UNVERIFIED)

An optimization algorithm that builds an approximate picture of the curvature of a function from the last few steps taken, rather than storing the full curvature matrix. Storing that matrix is impossible when there are hundreds of thousands of variables, as in a large molecular system. Keeping only recent history gives most of the benefit at a fraction of the memory. (UNVERIFIED)

A minimization algorithm that uses curvature information about the energy surface to choose each step, computing that information only approximately and stopping the approximation early. Using curvature converges in far fewer steps than using slope alone, and computing it exactly would be impossible for a large system. Stopping early is the compromise the name refers to. (UNVERIFIED)

An enhanced sampling algorithm is a computational procedure that modifies a standard simulation to accelerate the exploration of a molecule's possible states or to observe rare events. These algorithms are designed to overcome the high energy barriers that can trap a simulation in a single state for a long time.

An enhanced sampling algorithm where multiple independent simulation replicas (walkers) simultaneously explore the conformational space and contribute to a single, shared biasing potential. This parallelization significantly accelerates the convergence of methods like metadynamics or adaptive biasing force.

The IUPAC International Chemical Identifier (InChI) is a standardized text string that provides a unique, machine-readable signature for a specific chemical substance. It is algorithmically generated from a molecule's structural information and it is sensitive to its chirality, ensuring that a given compound will always produce the same identifier regardless of how it is drawn. This code serves as a universal label for linking chemical information across different databases and software.

The ICOSA algorithm is a computational method used to rapidly calculate the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) of a molecule. It works by placing a sphere of dots, arranged in a pattern based on an icosahedron, around each atom and then counting how many of these dots are not covered by neighboring atoms. This numerical approach provides a fast and efficient way to estimate the molecular surface area, a property that is crucial for implicit solvent models and for analyzing a molecule's exposure to its environment.

A minimization algorithm that moves the atoms at each step in the direction of the force on them, which is the steepest downhill direction from where they are. It is robust and almost never fails, because that direction always lowers the energy. It slows to a crawl in a long narrow valley, where the steepest direction points across the valley rather than along it. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that identifies which parts of a protein form regular repeating shapes, such as helices and sheets, from the coordinates of its backbone. It works by finding the pattern of hydrogen bonds between backbone groups, or by examining backbone angles. It is what turns a list of coordinates into the helix-and-arrow picture of a protein. (UNVERIFIED)

The DSSP (Define Secondary Structure of Proteins) algorithm is the most widely used and standard algorithm for assigning secondary structure to the residues of a protein. It works by identifying the characteristic hydrogen-bonding patterns between the backbone amide and carbonyl groups that define alpha-helices and beta-sheets. The detailed, per-residue output of the DSSP algorithm is a standard tool for protein structure analysis and validation.

OBSOLETE. A trajectory analysis algorithm is a computational procedure that processes the time-series of atomic coordinates from a simulation to calculate a specific property. These algorithms are the engines of analysis tools, turning raw simulation output into interpretable scientific data. For experts, this includes the specific algorithms for tasks like imaging periodic trajectories, calculating correlation functions, or clustering conformations.

comments: candidate for removal per https://github.com/CPCLab/molsim-ontology/issues/21

definition.val: A specialized algorithm for visualizing molecules in a periodic simulation box that ensures chemical bonds are always drawn correctly, even when they cross a boundary. It treats the periodic box as a torus (a donut shape), so that when a molecule is viewed, its connectivity is preserved without being artificially "broken" at the box edges. This scheme is important for creating clear and unambiguous visualizations of molecular structures and their interactions within a periodic environment. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that draws a smooth curve through a set of points by fitting a cubic polynomial between each neighbouring pair and matching their slopes and curvatures where they join. The matching is what stops the curve having visible corners. It is how a free energy profile is drawn from values computed at discrete points. (UNVERIFIED)

A method that decomposes a signal into contributions at each frequency and each moment at once, by matching it against a shape that is stretched and shifted across the data. A plain frequency analysis gives no information about when. That matters for a trajectory, where a motion may appear only during part of the run. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that applies the methods of statistics to summarise data, estimate a quantity, or judge how reliable a result is. Simulation output is a sample rather than an exact answer, so every number taken from it needs one. Reporting a value without an uncertainty is the most common failure this addresses. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical algorithm that estimates the distribution behind a set of points by placing a small smooth bump on each and adding them together. It assumes no particular shape for the distribution, unlike fitting a named family. How wide the bumps are decides whether it reveals real structure or smooths it away. (UNVERIFIED)

A residue name is a standardized short code, typically three or four letters, used in structure files to identify a specific type of molecular building block. For example, 'ALA' is the residue name for the amino acid alanine, and 'DG' can represent a deoxyguanosine nucleotide.

A short code identifying a particular sugar in the GLYCAM carbohydrate force field, encoding not only which sugar it is but which of its hydroxyl groups are linked onward. Sugars branch, so the same sugar appears in many linkage patterns and each needs its own template. That is why the naming carries linkage information where amino acid codes do not. (UNVERIFIED)

An atom name is a unique label given to an atom within a specific residue to distinguish it from other atoms of the same element. For example, in an amino acid, the names 'CA' and 'CB' are used to differentiate the alpha-carbon from the beta-carbon.

The atom of a residue designated to form the bond joining it to the neighbouring residue in a chain. Building a polymer from residue templates requires knowing which atom on each side makes that bond. Without it, templates could be listed in order and never joined. (UNVERIFIED)

The atom of a residue template that bonds to the preceding residue in a chain. In a protein it is the backbone nitrogen. Together with the tail atom it defines the direction in which templates are joined. (UNVERIFIED)

The atom of a residue template that bonds to the following residue in a chain. In a protein it is the backbone carbonyl carbon. A template with no tail atom defined cannot be followed by another, which is how a chain terminus is expressed. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. Miller indices are a set of three integers (h, k, l) that uniquely describe the orientation of a plane of atoms within a crystal lattice. These indices are determined from the positions of the spots in an X-ray diffraction pattern and are fundamental to crystallography. They are used to define the specific crystal faces and to calculate the theoretical diffraction pattern from a structural model.

comments: Marked for removal. See: https://github.com/CPCLab/molsim-ontology/issues/26

definition.val: A classification recorded in a topology stating what general kind of building block a residue is, such as protein, nucleic acid, water, ion or solvent. Analysis tools use it to select parts of a system without naming every residue. A mis-set value makes a selection quietly omit or include the wrong atoms. (UNVERIFIED)

A constituent part of a 3-dimensional data map, being either a grid point or the value stored at it. The grid points fix where the map is sampled and the values say what was found there. The term exists so that the 2 can be referred to separately. (UNVERIFIED)

A single cell of a 3-dimensional grid, holding one value for the small volume of space it covers. It is to a volume what a pixel is to an image. Analyses that map a property through space, such as where water sits around a protein, report their results one of these at a time. (UNVERIFIED)
A classification assigned to an atom to describe its fundamental chemical identity or its specific physical and computational properties within a molecular model.

comments: Previous definition: An atom type is a classification assigned to an atom in a force field that defines its interaction parameters based on its chemical environment. It encodes not just the chemical element but also its hybridization state and bonding pattern, so a carbonyl carbon will have a different atom type than an aromatic carbon.

definition.val: A description of an atom's surroundings used by a machine-learned force field, computed from the positions of its neighbours rather than assigned from a table. A conventional atom type is a fixed label such as "aromatic carbon"; this instead varies continuously with the local geometry. That is what lets such a model describe environments it was never given a label for. (UNVERIFIED)

A code identifying an amino acid that has been chemically altered, such as by phosphorylation or methylation. The standard 3-letter codes cover only the 20 unmodified residues, so a modified one needs a code of its own. The code is what links the residue to the extra parameters its modification requires. (UNVERIFIED)

A path image is a single, discrete snapshot or structure that represents one point along a continuous pathway between two molecular states. A collection of these images is used in methods like the Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) to map out a reaction path or conformational transition.

Trajectory post-processing is the general process of cleaning and preparing raw simulation trajectory files before performing detailed scientific analysis. This typically involves essential steps like removing the overall rotation and translation of a target molecule to keep it centered, and fixing any molecules that appear "broken" by the periodic boundary conditions. These routine procedures are necessary to create a clean trajectory that is suitable for correct visualization and accurate calculation of structural properties.

A system preparation stage in which a correspondence is established between the atoms of 2 structures, saying which atom of one plays the part of which atom of the other. An alchemical transformation needs it to know which atoms change and which stay. A wrong correspondence produces a calculation that runs to completion and gives a wrong answer. (UNVERIFIED)

A preparation process that produces the 2 files a simulation needs: a topology file saying what the system is made of, and a coordinate file saying where everything currently is. The topology lists the atoms, the bonds between them and the force field parameters, and it does not change during the run. The coordinates change at every step, which is why the 2 are kept apart. (UNVERIFIED)

The random tumbling of a molecule in a liquid, caused by collisions with the solvent around it. How fast it tumbles depends on its size and shape and on how viscous the solvent is. It is what NMR relaxation measurements are sensitive to, which is how a simulated value can be checked. (UNVERIFIED)

A modelling method that rebuilds an all-atom structure from a coarse-grained one, placing the atoms each grouped site stands for. Information was discarded when the coarse model was built, so the rebuilt atoms are a plausible arrangement rather than a recovered one. It is used to inspect a coarse-grained result in atomic detail, or to continue a simulation at finer resolution. (UNVERIFIED)

NMR refinement is a computational process used to generate or improve a three-dimensional model of a molecule using experimental data from Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. The method involves finding a structure, or an ensemble of structures, that is both stereochemically realistic and consistent with a set of experimental restraints, such as distances between atoms derived from the Nuclear Overhauser Effect. This process is essential for translating the raw data from an NMR experiment into a high-resolution atomic model.

A system preparation stage in which a molecular system is assembled and given force field parameters, producing the topology and coordinate files a simulation needs. It covers loading the structure, choosing the force field, adding solvent and counter-ions, and writing the output. It is the step at which a structure becomes a simulatable system. (UNVERIFIED)

A procedure applied at intervals during a simulation that subtracts any overall translation, and sometimes rotation, of the whole system. Small numerical errors accumulate into a drift of the entire box, which would otherwise be counted as thermal motion and inflate the temperature. Removing it keeps the reported temperature meaning what it should. (UNVERIFIED)

A chemical change made to a protein after it has been built from its amino acid sequence, such as attaching a phosphate, a sugar or a lipid. It can switch the protein's activity on or off, mark it for destruction, or send it to a particular part of the cell. Standard force fields do not include the modified residues, so extra parameters are needed to simulate one. (UNVERIFIED)

A post-translational modification in which a branched sugar chain is attached to the nitrogen of an asparagine side chain. It is among the most common modifications of proteins on the cell surface and of secreted proteins. The sugar chains are large, flexible and highly variable, which makes them among the hardest parts of a protein to simulate. (UNVERIFIED)

A post-translational modification in which sugars are attached to the oxygen of a serine or threonine side chain, added one at a time rather than as a preassembled block. Because they are added singly, the resulting chains vary far more between copies of the same protein than the nitrogen-linked kind. That variability is what makes such proteins hard to define, let alone simulate. (UNVERIFIED)

A model specifying the mathematical form assumed for the many-electron wavefunction in a quantum chemistry calculation, such as a single determinant or a combination of several configurations. It fixes what electronic structure the calculation is able to represent before any basis set is chosen. A single determinant cannot describe bond breaking or a near-degenerate ground state. (UNVERIFIED)

A wavefunction model in which every occupied molecular orbital holds exactly 2 electrons of opposite spin. It applies to molecules with no unpaired electrons, which is most stable organic molecules in their ground state. It is the default assumption of a quantum chemistry calculation unless an open-shell model is asked for. (UNVERIFIED)

A type of wavefunction model specifically used for molecules that have unpaired electrons, such as radicals or certain metal complexes. In an unrestricted open-shell wavefunction, electrons with spin-up and spin-down are allowed to occupy different spatial orbitals, providing the necessary flexibility to describe the different distributions of the unpaired electrons. This model is the basis for Unrestricted Hartree-Fock (UHF) and open-shell DFT calculations and is essential for correctly modeling the electronic structure and properties of radical species. (UNVERIFIED)

A regular, repeating local shape that a stretch of a protein or nucleic acid chain folds into, held together by hydrogen bonds between nearby parts of the backbone. In proteins the common ones are the helix and the sheet; in nucleic acids they include the double helix and the hairpin. It is local, so one chain contains many such stretches with irregular regions between them. (UNVERIFIED)

A beta sheet is a common shape in proteins where parts of the amino acid chain line up side-by-side like ribbons in a flat, pleated sheet. It is a secondary structure motif formed by two or more extended polypeptide chains, called beta-strands, which are linked laterally by a regular pattern of hydrogen bonds between their backbone atoms. These sheet structures form the rigid core of many proteins and are critical for creating binding surfaces for other molecules. (UNVERIFIED)

A parallel beta sheet is a type of beta sheet where the adjacent protein chains all run in the same direction, like lanes on a one-way highway. In this arrangement, the neighboring beta-strands are all aligned in the same N-terminus to C-terminus direction, which results in a pattern of angled, evenly spaced hydrogen bonds between the strands. This arrangement is typically found buried in the core of a protein and often requires long loop connections between the strands.

An anti-parallel beta sheet is a type of beta sheet where the adjacent protein strands run in opposite directions, like traffic on a two-way street. In this arrangement, the neighboring beta-strands are aligned in opposite N-terminus to C-terminus directions, resulting in a pattern of straight, perpendicular hydrogen bonds between the strands. This arrangement is generally more stable than the parallel form and is a very common structural motif found in many proteins.

OBSOLETE. A helix is a common shape in proteins and DNA where the molecular chain is twisted into a spiral or corkscrew. It is a secondary structure motif characterized by a repeating pattern of backbone dihedral angles that causes the polymer chain to follow a helical path, which is stabilized by a regular pattern of internal hydrogen bonds. The alpha-helix in proteins and the double helix of DNA are two of the most fundamental and recognizable structures in biology.

comments: Retired 2026-08-05 in favour of the Sequence Ontology term, which covers the same concept in the ontology whose scope owns protein secondary structure. The MOLSIM hierarchy position is preserved: the SO class is asserted under MOLSIM:001781 secondary structure so the DSSP category set stays in one place.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. The 3-10 helix is a type of spiral shape found in proteins that is tighter and more narrow than the common alpha-helix. It is a secondary structure motif characterized by a repeating hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of a residue and the backbone amide of the residue three positions down the chain (i → i+3). While less common than the alpha-helix, short segments of 3-10 helix are often found at the ends of alpha-helices, acting as a cap to the structure.

comments: Retired 2026-08-05 in favour of the Sequence Ontology term, which covers the same concept in the ontology whose scope owns protein secondary structure. The MOLSIM hierarchy position is preserved: the SO class is asserted under MOLSIM:001781 secondary structure so the DSSP category set stays in one place.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. The alpha-helix is the most common spiral shape found in proteins, resembling a coiled ribbon. It is a right-handed secondary structure motif characterized by a repeating hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of a residue and the backbone amide of the residue four positions down the chain (i → i+4). This highly stable and common structure forms a fundamental building block for the architecture of most proteins.

comments: Retired 2026-08-05 in favour of the Sequence Ontology term, which covers the same concept in the ontology whose scope owns protein secondary structure. The MOLSIM hierarchy position is preserved: the SO class is asserted under MOLSIM:001781 secondary structure so the DSSP category set stays in one place.

definition.val: OBSOLETE. The pi-helix is a wide spiral shape found in proteins that is less stable than the common alpha-helix. It is a secondary structure motif characterized by a repeating hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of a residue and the backbone amide of the residue five positions down the chain (i → i+5). Because its internal packing is less favorable, the pi-helix is usually found only as a short, single-turn insertion within other helical structures. Once thought to be rare, short π-helices are found in 15% of known protein structures and are believed to be an evolutionary adaptation derived by the insertion of a single amino acid into an α-helix.

comments: Retired 2026-08-05 in favour of the Sequence Ontology term, which covers the same concept in the ontology whose scope owns protein secondary structure. The MOLSIM hierarchy position is preserved: the SO class is asserted under MOLSIM:001781 secondary structure so the DSSP category set stays in one place.

definition.val: A secondary structure element in which 3 to 5 residues reverse the direction of a protein chain over a short distance. It is what lets 2 stretches of chain run back alongside each other, so a compact fold is possible at all. Without turns a chain could only extend. (UNVERIFIED)

A bend is a region in a protein chain that creates a sharp turn, changing the direction of the polypeptide. It is a short structural motif, typically involving a few amino acid residues, that is characterized by a specific pattern of backbone dihedral angles that reverses the direction of the chain.

A backbone conformation in which a polypeptide segment is stretched into a flat zig-zag, with backbone dihedral angles near the fully extended region of the Ramachandran plot. It is the conformation a strand takes inside a beta sheet, and the most extended a polypeptide reaches. The zig-zag is what places successive side chains on alternating faces. (UNVERIFIED)
A beta bridge is an isolated, localized hydrogen bond between two amino acid residues from different segments of a protein, mimicking the interactions found in β-sheets.

A conformational transition is the process where a molecule changes from one stable three-dimensional molecular arrangement to another. This can be a large-scale event, such as a protein switching between an active and an inactive state, or a more local change like the flipping of a sugar ring. Studying these transitions is fundamental to understanding how molecular function is controlled by changes in structure.

A crankshaft motion refers to a specific, localized, correlated movement of a protein's backbone. Specifically, it is an oscillation or rotation of a rigid peptide plane along an axis defined by two adjacent Cα carbon atoms.

The Solvent MoDeL (MDL) file is an explicit molecular model input used for 1D-RISM and 3D-RISM (Reference Interaction Site Model) calculations in software like Amber. It supplies atomic coordinates, partial charges, and Lennard-Jones parameters for solvent molecules or ions.

In computational chemistry and molecular dynamics, the mean solvation force is the average net force exerted by solvent molecules on a solute molecule, with all solvent degrees of freedom thermally averaged out. It represents the derivative of the potential of mean force (PMF) and drives conformational changes and structural binding in liquids.

The atom position is the precise location of an atom in three-dimensional space. It is described by a set of three Cartesian coordinates (X, Y, Z) that specify its location relative to a defined origin. The collection of all atom positions for a molecule at a given instant constitutes a single "frame" of a simulation trajectory, and the evolution of these positions over time is the fundamental output of a molecular dynamics simulation.

An interaction energy component arising when a small amount of electron density moves from one molecule to another at close range. It is a quantum mechanical effect that a force field with fixed atomic charges cannot represent, yet it contributes measurably to hydrogen bonds and to interactions with metal ions. Capturing it needs a polarizable force field or a quantum mechanical treatment. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy chosen as the zero point against which other energies in a calculation are reported. In a free energy calculation it is usually a known or simplified state, and every other state is quoted as a difference from it. Comparisons between systems are meaningless unless the same choice was made for both. (UNVERIFIED)

A physical property is a measurable characteristic of a substance or system that describes its physical state, such as its temperature, pressure, or density. In molecular simulations, these properties are calculated as averages over the course of the trajectory to describe the macroscopic state of the simulated system. These calculated properties are the primary outputs used to validate a simulation against experimental data and to understand the material characteristics of the molecular model.

A quantity giving how strongly a single atom scatters a wave, as a function of scattering angle. It rises with the number of electrons the atom has and falls as the angle increases, because the electron cloud has finite size. It is the per-atom term that structure factors are built from. (UNVERIFIED)

A program written in a language that is interpreted as it runs rather than compiled first, used to drive a sequence of steps automatically. Being interpreted makes it quick to change and slow to execute, which suits work that is mostly waiting on other programs. Most of the workflow around a simulation is scripts rather than compiled code. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy arising from the forces between 2 or more separate molecules, or between distinct parts of 1 molecule, computed as the energy of the whole minus the sum of the energies of the parts held at the same geometry. It gathers the electrostatic and van der Waals contributions into a single number. It measures how strongly the parts are held together, but it is not a free energy, because it contains no entropy. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy between a solute and all the water molecules around it. It sums the electrostatic and van der Waals contributions over every solute-water pair. Following it through a trajectory shows how the solute's contact with water changes as it moves. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy summing the interactions of every water molecule with every other water molecule in a system. It measures how strongly the solvent holds itself together, separately from anything the solute does. Changes in it are how the cost of opening a cavity for a solute is seen. (UNVERIFIED)

The REMD round-trip time is a diagnostic metric that measures how long it takes for a single simulation copy to travel through the full range of temperatures in a Replica Exchange Molecular Dynamics simulation. In this method, multiple simulations are run at different temperatures, and this metric tracks the time for one replica to go from the lowest to the highest temperature and back again. A short round-trip time indicates that the simulation is sampling conformations efficiently, which is necessary to obtain reliable results.

Lifetime curve data is a graph that shows how long a specific molecular interaction, such as a hydrogen bond, typically lasts in a simulation. The curve usually plots the probability that an interaction, once formed, will still exist after a certain amount of time has passed. This data is generated by calculating the autocorrelation function of an interaction's existence over a trajectory, and fitting the curve provides a characteristic lifetime for that interaction.

An average taken over a window that moves along a series, giving one value for each position of the window. It removes short-term fluctuation so that a slower trend can be seen. The width of the window sets what counts as fluctuation and what counts as trend. (UNVERIFIED)

A measure of how far 2 sets of collective modes span the same motions, computed from the inner products between their eigenvectors. A value near 1 means the 2 sets describe the same motion, and a value near 0 means they do not. It is how the modes from 2 simulations, or from a simulation and an experiment, are compared. (UNVERIFIED)

A single number summarising how strongly the parts of a molecule move together, computed as the root mean square of all the pairwise correlation values. It reduces a whole correlation matrix to 1 figure, so 2 simulations can be compared directly. It says how much correlated motion there is but not where. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantity giving the average interaction energy between a solute and the solvent at each point in the space around it, stored on a 3-dimensional grid. Negative regions mark positions where a solvent molecule is held, positive regions mark positions it avoids. It differs from a density map in reporting energy rather than how often solvent is found. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantity giving, at each point of a 3-dimensional grid, the average interaction energy between solvent molecules there. Comparing it with the bulk value shows where a solute has disturbed the solvent's own structure. Regions where solvent holds itself together less well than in the bulk are where a ligand can most easily displace it. (UNVERIFIED)

An energy giving the average electrostatic interaction of a single solvent molecule with all the other solvent molecules, obtained by dividing the total solvent-solvent energy by the number of solvent molecules. Normalising this way makes the value comparable between systems holding different amounts of solvent. Without it, a larger box simply reports a larger number. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantity giving the average electrostatic energy of the solvent at each point of a 3-dimensional grid, computed with particle mesh Ewald. It shows where the solvent is electrostatically stabilised and where it is strained. It differs from a solvent density map in reporting energy rather than how much solvent is present. (UNVERIFIED)

An interaction energy giving the average interaction of a single water molecule with its neighbours, obtained by dividing the total water-water energy by the number of water molecules. Dividing this way makes systems containing different amounts of water comparable. A shift in it marks water that is more or less strongly bound than in the bulk. (UNVERIFIED)

A quantity giving the average direction and size of molecular dipoles at each point of a 3-dimensional grid. It shows how solvent molecules orient themselves around a solute, which a plain density map cannot. Regions where the dipoles all point the same way mark strong local electric fields. (UNVERIFIED)

A measure of how crowded the surroundings of an atom or molecule are, given as the number of neighbours within a chosen distance. It is the simplest description of local packing. Comparing it with the bulk value shows where a structure is more or less tightly packed than usual. (UNVERIFIED)

A measure of how many molecules sit near a chosen point, divided by how many would be expected there if they were spread evenly. A value above 1 means molecules gather at that point and below 1 means they avoid it. Dividing out the expected number is what makes values at different distances comparable. (UNVERIFIED)

A measure of how closely the 4 nearest neighbours of a water molecule sit at the corners of a regular tetrahedron around it. Water in its ordinary hydrogen-bonded network is close to tetrahedral, and disruption shows as a fall in the value. It is how water near a surface or an ion is shown to be structured differently from bulk water. (UNVERIFIED)

A tetrahedral order parameter rescaled to run from −1/3 to 1, where 1 is a perfect tetrahedron and 0 is a random arrangement. The rescaling puts the value of random water at 0, so a number can be read directly as how much more ordered than random the arrangement is. It is the form usually reported. (UNVERIFIED)

A chemical shift restraint simulation is a method where experimental Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) chemical shifts are used to guide a molecular dynamics simulation. An additional energy term is added that penalizes the simulation if the back-calculated chemical shifts from the trajectory do not agree with the experimental values. For experts, this method is a powerful tool for refining the accuracy of a structural ensemble to be consistent with experimental NMR data.

A pseudocontact shift restraint simulation is a technique that uses a specific type of NMR data, known as pseudocontact shifts (PCS), to guide a simulation. PCS provide long-range distance and angular information relative to a paramagnetic metal center in the molecule. For structural biologists, using PCS restraints is a powerful method for determining the structure and dynamics of proteins and their complexes.

A direct dipolar coupling restraint simulation is a method that incorporates experimental NMR data from residual dipolar couplings (RDCs) to guide a MD simulation. RDCs provide information about the orientation of chemical bonds relative to an external magnetic field.

nodes.lbl: residual chemical shift anisotropy restraint simulation

definition.val: A residual chemical shift anisotropy (RCSA) restraint simulation is a technique that uses NMR RCSA data to guide a MD simulation. RCSA provides information about the orientation of the chemical shift tensor for specific atoms, which is sensitive to local structure and dynamics.

A value printed in a simulation's energy output that tracks part of the algorithm rather than any physical interaction. Thermostats and barostats that add extra degrees of freedom to the system report these, so that a conserved total can still be checked. Adding such a value into a reported potential energy is a common and silent error. (UNVERIFIED)

An electrostatic method that represents the solvent beyond a cutoff distance as a uniform medium that polarizes in response to the charges inside, rather than as individual molecules. The polarized medium pushes back with a field that is added to the direct interactions. It is much cheaper than Ewald summation and less accurate, particularly for a system carrying a net charge. (UNVERIFIED)

A collective variable is a simplified coordinate that helps describe a complex process in a simulation, such as the distance between two proteins as they bind. Instead of tracking thousands of atomic coordinates, a collective variable reduces the system's motion to one or a few key parameters that capture the essence of the event. These variables are frequently used in enhanced sampling methods to focus computational effort on exploring a specific conformational change or reaction pathway.

A distance collective variable is a simple coordinate that measures the separation between two specific atoms or groups of atoms. It is one of the most common variables used in simulations to track processes like a drug molecule unbinding from its target protein. Monitoring this distance provides a straightforward way to follow the progress of an association or dissociation event.

nodes.lbl: center of mass distance collective variable

definition.val: A center of mass distance collective variable measures the separation between the centers of mass of two groups of atoms, such as two entire proteins or a protein and a ligand. This provides a robust measure of the distance between whole molecular entities, averaging out the fast motions of individual atoms.

nodes.lbl: difference of center of mass distances collective variable

definition.val: This is a complex coordinate that tracks the difference between two separate center-of-mass distance measurements. It defines a reaction coordinate by calculating the absolute difference between two distinct COM distance measurements.

nodes.lbl: linear combination of distances collective variable

definition.val: A linear combination of distances is a mathematical expression used in molecular simulations to define a collective variable (CV). It sums or subtracts multiple specific atomic distances, each multiplied by a defined weight, creating a single reaction coordinate to track conformational changes like folding or chemical reactions.

An angle collective variable is a low-dimensional geometric descriptor that measures the angle formed by three specific atoms or groups of atoms during a simulation. This variable is used to monitor hinge-like motions, such as the opening and closing of domains in a protein.

nodes.lbl: center of mass angle collective variable

definition.val: A center of mass angle collective variable measures the angle formed by the centers of mass of three distinct groups of atoms. This is useful for describing the large-scale orientation of entire protein domains or molecules relative to one another, smoothing out the rapid fluctuations of individual atoms.

A torsion collective variable is a coordinate that tracks the value of a specific dihedral angle, which describes the rotation around a chemical bond. These variables are fundamental for describing the detailed three-dimensional shape of a flexible molecule. They are often used in enhanced sampling simulations to accelerate the rotation of protein side chains or to explore different backbone conformations.

nodes.lbl: center of mass torsion collective variable

definition.val: A center of mass torsion collective variable is a dihedral angle defined by the centers of mass of four distinct groups of atoms, rather than four single atoms. This allows for the description of torsional or twisting motions between large molecular domains or subunits.

nodes.lbl: sum of cosines of dihedrals collective variable

definition.val: This is a collective variable created by summing the cosine values of several different dihedral angles within a molecule. This mathematical combination creates a smooth, continuous variable that describes the collective rotational state of multiple bonds at once. It is often used in enhanced sampling methods to create a simplified coordinate that captures a complex, multi-dimensional conformational change.

nodes.lbl: sum of sines of dihedrals collective variable

definition.val: This is a collective variable created by summing the sine values of several different dihedral angles within a molecule. This mathematical combination creates a smooth, continuous variable that describes the collective rotational state of multiple bonds at once. It is often used in enhanced sampling methods to create a simplified coordinate that captures a complex, multi-dimensional conformational change.

A paired dihedral collective variable is a coordinate that combines two different dihedral angles, often the phi and psi backbone angles of a protein, into a single analysis. This is most commonly used to generate a two-dimensional free energy map, known as a Ramachandran plot, which reveals the energetically allowed conformations of the protein backbone. This analysis is fundamental for understanding protein structure and flexibility.

A pattern dihedral is a specialized Collective Variable (CV) used in MD to track the conformational transitions of a molecular system, such as protein folding or crystal polymorphs. It measures a weighted linear combination of multiple specific dihedral angles to act as a low-dimensional structural parameter, often replacing a complex set of atomic coordinates.

The radius of gyration is a collective variable that measures the overall compactness of a molecule or a group of atoms. It quantifies how spread out the atoms are from the molecule's center of mass, with a smaller value indicating a more compact shape. This variable is commonly used as a simple metric to monitor large-scale conformational changes, such as the process of a protein folding into its native structure or unfolding.

A multi-RMSD collective variable is a coordinate that simultaneously measures a molecule's structural similarity to several different reference structures. This is useful for tracking a molecule's transitions between multiple known functional states, such as an active, inactive, and an intermediate conformation. By monitoring which reference structure the molecule is closest to, this variable can map out the complex conformational landscape connecting different states.

A number of bonds collective variable is a coordinate that counts the number of specific chemical bonds that exist at any given moment in a simulation. This variable is only meaningful when using a reactive force field that allows chemical bonds to form and break. It serves as a simple and direct way to track the progress of a chemical reaction by monitoring the creation or destruction of key covalent bonds.

A handedness collective variable is a mathematical measure that quantifies the chirality, or "handedness," of a molecular structure, such as the left-handed versus right-handed twist of a helix. This variable provides a continuous value that can track a molecule's transition between different chiral states during a simulation.

A complex quantity describing how strongly and with what phase a crystal scatters a wave in a given direction, summed over the atoms in its repeating unit. Its magnitude is what a diffraction experiment measures; its phase is not, which is the central difficulty of crystallography. The electron density follows from both by Fourier transform. (UNVERIFIED)

The physical components of a computer system on which software runs: processors, memory, storage and the networks between machines. It is recorded alongside a simulation because how long the work took, and sometimes whether it is bit-for-bit reproducible, depends on it. The scientific result should not depend on it, and a difference between machines is a sign of a problem. (UNVERIFIED)

A parameter giving the effective size of an atom, as the distance at which another atom begins to be repelled strongly. It is the radius of the hard sphere that best represents where Pauli repulsion overtakes the weak attraction between 2 non-bonded atoms. These radii set the molecular surface used in solvation models and in most measures of packing. (UNVERIFIED)

The Larmor frequency is the specific rate at which a magnetic particle, like an atomic nucleus, wobbles or "precesses" when placed in a strong external magnetic field. This is analogous to the way a spinning top wobbles in the Earth's gravitational field. This frequency is the fundamental principle behind all Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) experiments, as it determines the exact frequency of energy the nucleus will absorb.

A function that varies smoothly between 0 and 1 across a shell of space, used to blend an atom's quantum and classical descriptions as it crosses the boundary. Blending removes the jump in energy that an abrupt reassignment would cause. The width of the shell trades smoothness against how many atoms are in a mixed state at once. (UNVERIFIED)

A data analysis method that tests whether a simulation has run long enough for the quantity of interest to stop drifting. It follows a chosen property, such as total energy or a structural measure, and checks whether its running average settles over the later part of the trajectory. Without it, a reported average may reflect only the part of the trajectory that happened to be sampled. (UNVERIFIED)

A modeling and setup tool is a type of software used to construct and prepare a molecular system before a simulation is run. This involves tasks like building a molecule from scratch, repairing a structure from an experimental database, or surrounding a protein with water molecules to mimic its natural environment. For an expert, these tools are essential for creating a chemically correct and physically stable starting point, which is a prerequisite for any meaningful simulation.

A software program that performs a simulation itself, computing the forces on every atom and advancing their positions step by step. It takes a prepared system and a set of parameters and produces a trajectory. Everything else in a simulation workflow either prepares its input or analyses its output. (UNVERIFIED)

A dynamics analysis method that reduces the motion in a trajectory to the few collective movements that account for most of the total fluctuation, using principal component analysis. The largest components are usually functionally meaningful, such as hinge bending between domains, while the smallest are thermal noise. It lets a trajectory of thousands of coordinates be discussed in terms of 2 or 3 motions. (UNVERIFIED)

A matrix whose entry at row i and column j gives the correlation between the fluctuations of quantities i and j. In trajectory analysis the quantities are usually the displacements of atoms or residues, so the matrix says which parts of the molecule move together. It is the input from which correlated motion and network analyses are computed. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis method that identifies which parts of a molecule are rigid and which move, usually by computing the root-mean-square fluctuation of each atom or residue about its average position. The result separates a stable core from mobile loops and termini. It is also what simulated values are compared against experimental B-factors with. (UNVERIFIED)

A contact map is a simplified 2D picture that shows which parts of a molecule are touching other parts of itself or other molecules. Contact maps provide a representation of molecular interactions or a protein foldings.

A contact map recording which pairs of atoms or residues are in contact in a reference folded structure. It is built once from an experimental structure and then used as the benchmark a simulated conformation is scored against. The fraction of its contacts that a conformation reproduces is the usual measure of how folded that conformation is. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-native contact map is a contact map that shows the atomic touches in a misfolded or unfolded protein structure that are not present in its correct, functional shape. It is used to identify incorrect or transient interactions that may form during a simulation, especially in the study of protein folding pathways or misfolded states. Analyzing non-native contacts is crucial for understanding the formation of misfolded intermediates and kinetic traps on the folding landscape. (UNVERIFIED)

Hydrophobic patches are clusters of non-polar, "water-fearing" atoms or amino acid side-chains that are exposed on the surface of a larger molecule, such as a protein. Because water molecules are highly polar, they are repelled by these non-polar regions and instead cluster together to interact with themselves.

A data analysis method that represents a molecule as a graph, with atoms or residues as nodes and interactions or correlations as edges, and then applies graph theory to it. It finds residues that act as hubs and traces paths of correlated motion between distant sites. It is the usual way to reason about allosteric communication and about the reach of a mutation. (UNVERIFIED)

A structural analysis method that finds cavities on or inside a molecule and measures their size, shape and how they change over time. A cavity that appears only briefly cannot be seen in a single experimental structure. Finding such transient cavities is one of the things simulation adds to a static structure. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that examines the behaviour of a small molecule bound to a larger one during a simulation. It covers how the ligand moves within its site, which contacts it makes and keeps, and whether it stays bound at all. It treats the ligand as the subject rather than as part of the system. (UNVERIFIED)

The complete set of hardware on which a simulation runs, from a single workstation to a large cluster. It is recorded because how long a simulation took, and sometimes whether it is exactly reproducible, depends on it. Results should not depend on it, and a difference between machines is a sign that something is wrong. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis method that characterises the pocket a ligand occupies, measuring its volume, shape and how that changes as the simulation proceeds. A pocket that opens and closes during a run cannot be judged from the single structure a crystal gives. It is how a binding site is shown to be druggable or transient. (UNVERIFIED)

Residence time is the average amount of time that a molecule, such as a water molecule or a ligand, spends in a specific, defined location, like a protein's binding site. It is calculated from a simulation by monitoring when a molecule enters a region and when it leaves, and then averaging this duration over many such events.

A confidence score produced by a structure prediction model for each residue, estimating how accurately that residue's position has been placed, on a scale from 0 to 100. It reports the model's confidence, not the accuracy of the structure, so a confident prediction can still be wrong. Regions scoring low are often genuinely disordered rather than badly predicted. (UNVERIFIED)

Backbone DH fluctuations are a measure of how much the backbone of a protein wiggles and changes shape during a simulation. It specifically quantifies the fluctuations in the dihedral angles (DH) of the protein's backbone, which describe the rotations around the chemical bonds that connect the amino acids. Analyzing these fluctuations provides a detailed picture of the protein's flexibility and dynamics that is independent of its overall tumbling motion.

Membrane analysis is a category of analysis methods specifically focused on characterizing the properties of lipid bilayer simulations. These methods are used to quantify the structural and dynamic behavior of the membrane itself and its interactions with other molecules, like embedded proteins. This includes calculating key properties such as the area per lipid, membrane thickness, and lipid order parameters to validate the simulation and understand membrane function.

The area per lipid is a fundamental biophysical metric representing the average cross-sectional surface area occupied by a single lipid molecule within a lipid bilayer. It is calculated by dividing the total area of the simulation box in the membrane plane by the number of lipids in one leaflet.

Lipid contact analysis is an analysis method used to identify and quantify the interactions between lipid molecules and a protein embedded in the membrane. The analysis tracks which specific lipid molecules are in close contact with the protein over the course of a simulation. This method may be used for identifying potential "hotspot" lipid binding sites on a membrane protein and understanding the composition of the annular lipid shell.

Lipid density is a measure of how tightly packed the lipid molecules are in a simulated cell membrane. It is typically calculated as a one-dimensional profile along the axis perpendicular to the membrane plane, showing the mass or electron density of different lipid components like headgroups and tails. Analyzing the lipid density profile is a fundamental check to ensure the simulated membrane has the correct structure and thickness, and it reveals how an embedded protein might locally perturb the lipid packing.

Lipid distribution refers to the spatial arrangement and composition of different types of lipid molecules within a simulated membrane. In a mixed bilayer, lipids are often not randomly distributed but can form distinct domains or clusters, and some lipids may preferentially accumulate around an embedded protein. Analyzing this distribution is crucial for understanding membrane organization and the specific lipid environment required for a membrane protein's function.

Lipid order parameters are a set of values that measure how well-aligned and ordered the flexible tails of lipid molecules are within a simulated cell membrane. A value of 1 means the lipid tail is perfectly straight and aligned perpendicular to the membrane surface, while a value of 0 means it is completely disordered. These parameters, specifically the deuterium order parameter (SCD), can be directly compared with experimental results from NMR spectroscopy, making them one of the most important metrics for validating the physical accuracy of a membrane simulation.

Membrane geometry describes the overall three-dimensional shape and dimensions of a simulated cell membrane. This includes properties like the membrane's thickness, its lateral dimensions in the simulation box, and its overall shape, which can be planar, curved, or even vesicular. Characterizing the membrane geometry is a fundamental part of analyzing membrane simulations, ensuring the system is stable and providing the context for the behavior of embedded proteins.

Membrane curvature is a measure of how much a simulated cell membrane is bent or curved. This property is calculated by fitting the positions of the lipid headgroups to a mathematical surface and then determining the local or average curvature of that surface. Analyzing membrane curvature is essential for studying processes like vesicle formation, membrane fusion, and the influence of proteins that induce or sense bending in the lipid bilayer.

The membrane width is the thickness of a simulated cell membrane, measured from one side to the other, along the z-axis. It is typically defined as the distance between the peaks in the density profile of the lipid headgroups or phosphate atoms on opposite sides of the bilayer. The membrane width is a key structural parameter that is monitored to confirm a simulation is properly equilibrated and is used to understand how membrane proteins match their hydrophobic length to the surrounding lipid environment.

The pore dimension refers to the size and shape of a channel or tunnel that passes through a protein. This property is calculated by finding the radius of the narrowest point (the constriction site) and the overall profile of the channel's radius along its length. Analyzing the pore dimensions is critical for understanding how ion channels and transporters function, as it determines which molecules are small enough to pass through the membrane.

DNA bendability is the intrinsic mechanical property that describes how easily a DNA double helix can deviate from its ideal straight conformation by adopting a bent or curved structure. This property depends on the nucleotide sequence, with some sequences being inherently more flexible than others. Sequence-dependent bendability plays a key role in DNA packaging, nucleosome formation, and protein-DNA recognition, as many proteins induce or stabilize DNA bending upon binding.

Base breathing refers to a specific and transient opening of one or more base pairs in a DNA or RNA double helix due to the temporary disruption of hydrogen bonds. During these events, the bases become transiently exposed to the surrounding solvent and more accessible without necessarily becoming fully unstacked from the helix. When this opening occurs at the ends of the duplex, it is commonly referred to as terminal fraying. These spontaneous opening events are a natural part of the helix's dynamics and are thought to be important for allowing proteins to access the genetic information encoded in the bases. Analyzing the frequency and duration of these motions provides insight into the local stability and accessibility of the DNA or RNA structure.

A helical parameter is one of a set of measurements that describe the detailed 3D shape of a DNA or RNA double helix. These parameters quantify the relative position and orientation of adjacent base pairs, including values for twist, roll, slide, and rise, which define the local helical geometry. Calculating these parameters from a simulation trajectory is the standard method for characterizing the sequence-dependent structure of nucleic acids and for distinguishing between different helical forms like A-DNA and B-DNA.

Inter-base pair (Inter-BP) correlation analysis refers to the statistical coupling between the structural parameters of neighboring DNA base pairs or base-pair steps. It quantifies how variations in one helical parameter (e.g., roll, twist, or slide) are associated with changes in the same or different parameters at adjacent base pairs. These correlations reveal sequence-dependent structural coupling and cooperative conformational behavior within the DNA double helix, providing insight into its flexibility, mechanics, and recognition by DNA-bining proteins.

Nucleic acid backbone flexibility is a measure of the ability of the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA or RNA to adopt different conformations through rotations about its backbone torsion angles. It is commonly characterized by analyzing the distributions and fluctuations during a simulation of the backbone dihedral angles (α, β, γ, δ, ε, ζ), the glycosidic angle (χ), and the sugar pucker. Backbone flexibility plays a fundamental role in determining the structural dynamics, mechanical properties, and biological functions of nucleic acids, influencing DNA bending and packaging as well as RNA folding and molecular recognition.

Nucleosome wrapping describes the way a long DNA molecule is spooled around a histone protein octamer, forming the fundamental repeating unit of chromatin. Studying nucleosome wrapping is essential for understanding how DNA is compacted and how access to the genetic code is regulated for gene expression.

A property giving how strongly a structure resists being deformed by an applied force. For a single bond or angle it is set by the force constant in the force field; for a whole molecule or assembly it emerges from the network of interactions. It is the inverse of flexibility and is measured in force per unit displacement. (UNVERIFIED)

A dynamics analysis method that identifies groups of atoms whose movements are correlated, so that they travel together as a unit rather than fluctuating independently. It picks out large-scale events such as a protein domain shifting or twisting as a whole. Those events are usually the ones that matter for function, such as an active site opening and closing. (UNVERIFIED)

Trajectory meta-analysis refers to a higher level of analysis that involves comparing, contrasting, or combining the results from multiple, independent simulation trajectories. This can be used to improve statistical certainty, assess the convergence of a simulation, or identify the differences in dynamics between a wild-type protein and a mutant. This approach is essential for drawing robust conclusions that are not dependent on a single simulation run.

Trajectory comparison is a specific type of meta-analysis where two or more simulation trajectories are quantitatively compared to identify similarities and differences in their conformational sampling. This is often done by calculating metrics that measure the overlap of the conformational ensembles or by projecting the trajectories onto a common free energy landscape. This method is used to rigorously assess the impact of a mutation or ligand binding on a protein's dynamics.

A molecular simulation system is the complete collection of all the molecules included in a computational model for a simulation. This includes the main molecule of interest, such as a protein, as well as all the surrounding solvent molecules, ions, and any other components.

A carbohydrate system is a type of molecular simulation system where the primary molecules being studied are carbohydrates. This can range from a single sugar molecule in water to a complex polysaccharide or the glycan portion of a glycoprotein. These systems require specialized force fields and analysis techniques to accurately model the unique stereochemistry and flexibility of glycosidic linkages.

A complex system in this context refers to a molecular simulation system that contains two or more interacting macromolecules, or a macromolecule interacting with a smaller molecule like a drug. The primary focus of simulating such a system is to study the interactions, binding, and functional consequences of the molecules coming together.

A ligand complex system is a type of complex system where the focus is on the interaction between a large macromolecule, such as a protein or DNA, and a smaller molecule, known as a ligand. These simulations are central to the field of drug discovery, where the goal is to understand how a potential drug molecule binds to its biological target.

A DNA-ligand system is a type of molecular simulation system where the primary molecules being studied are DNA molecules interacting with small molecule ligands. These simulations are used to study how drugs or other small molecules bind to DNA, which can be a mechanism for anti-cancer or anti-viral therapies. These systems are important for understanding intercalation, groove binding, and the structural changes induced in DNA upon ligand binding.

An RNA-ligand system is a type of molecular simulation system where the primary molecules being studied are RNA molecules interacting with small molecule ligands. With the growing recognition of RNA as a major drug target, these simulations are becoming increasingly important for discovering and designing new therapeutics. These systems are challenging due to the high flexibility of RNA and the often subtle nature of the binding interactions.

A molecular system consisting of a protein bound to a small molecule. It is the most commonly simulated kind of complex, because it is what drug binding is. What is usually studied is how tightly the 2 bind and which contacts hold them together. (UNVERIFIED)

A hybrid complex system is a type of complex system composed of macromolecules from different biological classes. This most commonly refers to a complex formed between a protein and a nucleic acid, such as a transcription factor bound to DNA. Simulating these systems is essential for understanding many fundamental biological processes like gene regulation and DNA repair.

A nucleic acid complex system is a type of molecular simulation system where the primary molecules being studied are two or more nucleic acid molecules. This can include a standard DNA double helix, an RNA duplex, or more complex structures like DNA-RNA hybrids or multi-stranded RNA junctions. These simulations are crucial for understanding the structure and stability of the genetic material and functional RNA molecules.

A DNA-DNA system is a type of molecular simulation system where the primary molecules being studied are two or more interacting strands of DNA.
