A validation analysis that checks recorded or extracted metadata for completeness, correctness, and internal consistency against expected schemas or physical constraints. It helps ensure that a simulation dataset is reliably described before it is shared or archived. (UNVERIFIED)
A trajectory post-processing that translates atomic coordinates back into the primary periodic unit cell.

A restrained simulation method that biases the dynamics using experimental nuclear magnetic resonance observables, such as interatomic distance restraints from nuclear Overhauser effects or torsion-angle restraints from scalar couplings. It guides the simulated structure toward conformations consistent with the measurements. (UNVERIFIED)

A restrained subset dynamics in which only a selected group of atoms is allowed to move while the remaining atoms are held fixed throughout the run. It reduces computational cost and focuses sampling on a region of interest, taking its name from the Amber convention of designating a mobile region. (UNVERIFIED)

An enhanced sampling parameter that specifies how often exchanges between neighboring replicas are attempted during a replica exchange simulation. It controls the rate at which configurations are swapped between conditions such as different temperatures. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration parameter that specifies how frequently the net translational motion of the system's center of mass is removed during a run. Periodic removal prevents the gradual accumulation of spurious overall drift of the simulated system. (UNVERIFIED)

An integration parameter that specifies how many short inner integration steps are taken per long outer step in a multiple-timestep integration scheme. It sets how often fast-varying forces are evaluated relative to slow-varying forces to improve computational efficiency. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation parameter that governs how frequently and in what form simulation data are written to output files during a run. It determines the temporal resolution and volume of the recorded energies, coordinates, and diagnostic information. (UNVERIFIED)

An output control parameter that specifies how often energy and related thermodynamic quantities are written to the output or log during a run. Smaller intervals give finer-grained monitoring at the cost of larger output files. (UNVERIFIED)

An output control parameter that specifies how often a restart file containing the current coordinates, velocities, and state is written during a run. It determines how much progress can be recovered if the run is interrupted. (UNVERIFIED)

An output control parameter that specifies how often diagnostic and status information is written to the simulation log during a run. It controls the verbosity and temporal resolution of the recorded run history. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation state that represents the elapsed model time reached by the system at a given point in a molecular dynamics run. It records how far the simulation has advanced along the physical time coordinate.

A thermodynamic property that represents the mass density of the simulated system at the end of a run or equilibration stage. It is commonly compared against experimental density to assess whether the system has equilibrated correctly. (UNVERIFIED)

A computed observable that quantifies the computational cost or efficiency of a simulation run rather than a physical property of the system. Examples include elapsed real time and the amount of simulated time produced per unit of computing time. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational performance metric that measures the total real-world elapsed time taken to complete a run from start to finish. It reflects the actual time a user waits, including all computation and input or output. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational performance metric that measures the cumulative processor time consumed by a run, summed across all active compute cores. It reflects total computational effort rather than elapsed real time. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational performance metric that measures the real-world elapsed time spent preparing a run before the production phase begins, such as reading inputs and building data structures. It isolates initialization overhead from the main computation.

A computational performance metric that measures the real-world elapsed time spent in the production phase of a simulation run, during which the trajectory of interest is generated. It excludes setup and finalization overhead.

A computational performance metric that represents the mean real-world time required to advance the simulation by one integration step. It is a convenient measure of per-step computational efficiency. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational performance metric that expresses how much simulated model time is produced per unit of real-world computing time, commonly reported as nanoseconds per day. It is a standard measure for comparing the practical speed of simulations. (UNVERIFIED)

A plan specification that describes a sequential, multi-stage computational workflow, such as minimization, heating, equilibration, and production, applied to a molecular system. It organizes the individual stages and their ordering into a single reproducible procedure. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular dynamics process that constitutes one discrete, chronological phase within a larger simulation run, characterized by its own role and its own input and output files. Examples include a heating stage or a production stage. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation parameter that specifies how another parameter, such as target temperature, restraint force constant, or non-bonded cutoff, changes over the course of a run, whether across simulated time or across integration steps. It captures ramping and stepwise schedules applied during a stage. (UNVERIFIED)

A validation analysis that evaluates whether two consecutive simulation stages join without an unexpected break, by comparing the end time of one stage with the start time of the next. It flags gaps that may indicate missing segments or unit errors. (UNVERIFIED)

A validation analysis that checks whether metadata extracted from several distinct files describing the same stage, such as topology, input, output, and trajectory files, agree with one another. It surfaces inconsistencies such as mismatched atom counts or timesteps. (UNVERIFIED)

An information content entity that records a failure, exception, or warning encountered while reading or extracting metadata from a simulation data file. It preserves the reason a file could not be fully processed. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that designates a specific standardized schema variant that a file adheres to within a broader container format, such as the AMBER conventions used inside a NetCDF file. It identifies the precise rules for interpreting the file's contents. (UNVERIFIED)

An information content entity that assigns a high-level descriptive category to a molecular system based on its overall composition, such as a protein-ligand complex in explicit water. It provides a concise, human-readable summary of what is being simulated. (UNVERIFIED)
An atom selection specification that defines a subset of atoms within a molecular system using a formal string or logical expression following the format of a specific software.

A simulation state time that represents the average amount of simulated time elapsed between consecutive saved frames of a trajectory. It reflects how finely the trajectory samples the simulated time coordinate. (UNVERIFIED)

A simulation state time that represents the difference between the end time of one simulation stage and the start time of the next. A nonzero gap indicates a break in the continuous simulated-time coordinate across stages. (UNVERIFIED)

An analysis algorithm that identifies which atoms in a molecular system are hydrogens, for the purpose of applying or detecting hydrogen mass repartitioning. Different strategies rely on different atomic attributes, such as atomic number or atom name. (UNVERIFIED)

A thermodynamic property that represents the mass density of the simulated system at the start of a run, computed from the topology mass and the initial periodic box volume. It provides a baseline for comparison against the equilibrated density reached during a constant-pressure run. (UNVERIFIED)

A cross-source validation that checks whether the atom count agrees across all files describing a system, such as topology, trajectory, etc. A mismatch indicates the files do not describe the same system.

A cross-source validation that checks whether periodic box information is consistently present or absent across the files describing a stage. It flags cases where, for example, a topology declares a box but a coordinate file does not. (UNVERIFIED)

A cross-source validation that checks whether step counts, timesteps, and total durations agree across the input, output, and trajectory files of a stage. It verifies that the recorded trajectory length matches the configured number of steps times the timestep. (UNVERIFIED)

A cross-source validation that checks whether the coordinate write frequency configured in the input matches the frequency reflected in the output and trajectory. It confirms that sampling settings were applied as specified. (UNVERIFIED)

A polypeptide domain that occurs in a protein. It is a distinct, self-contained part of a protein that folds up on its own and usually carries out a particular job. Large proteins are often built from several domains.
A protein domain whose function is to attach to a matching partner molecule called a receptor.
A protein domain that contains the active site, the pocket where an enzyme carries out its chemical reaction. It is the working part of an enzyme.

A system classification label that records the biological job of the main protein in a simulated system. Proteins do most of the work in living cells, and this label groups simulations by the kind of job their protein does. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein functional class label for a system whose main protein is an enzyme, a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction in the cell. Enzyme simulations usually centre on the active site, so they often need a quantum description of the reacting groups. Knowing that a system is an enzyme tells a reader what the simulation was most likely set up to look at. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein functional class label for a system whose main protein is a transport protein, one that moves ions or molecules from place to place. These almost always sit in a membrane, so the system will contain a lipid bilayer as well as water. The property of interest is usually a rate of passage rather than a structure. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein functional class label for a system whose main protein is a structural protein, one that gives shape, stiffness, or mechanical strength. These form long fibres or networks rather than compact globules, so a single copy is rarely the unit that matters. They are often studied with coarse-grained models for that reason. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein functional class label for a system whose main protein is a regulatory protein, one that switches biological processes on or off. What is usually simulated is the change between its active and inactive shapes. Such changes are often too slow to observe directly, so enhanced sampling is commonly needed. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein functional class label for a system whose main protein is a signaling protein, one that passes messages within a cell or between cells. Binding at one site frequently alters behaviour at a distant one, which is the allosteric behaviour such simulations set out to trace. Many are membrane receptors, so the system will include a bilayer. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein functional class label for a system whose main protein is a motor protein, one that turns chemical energy into movement. Their working cycle takes milliseconds or longer, far beyond what a direct simulation reaches, so they are studied in stages or with coarse-grained models. The coupling between chemistry at one site and motion elsewhere is the point of interest. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein functional class label for a system whose main protein is an immune protein, one that helps recognise or fight off germs and other threats. Simulations of these usually concern how tightly and how specifically a target is recognised. The binding surfaces are often flexible loops, which makes sampling them the main difficulty. (UNVERIFIED)

A protein functional class label for a system whose main protein is a storage protein, one that holds onto useful substances such as iron or amino acids until they are needed. They are usually large symmetric assemblies with a cavity inside. What is studied is how a substance enters, is held, and is released. (UNVERIFIED)

A system setup parameter that gives the three angles (commonly α, β, γ) between the edges of the simulation box. These are needed to describe boxes that are not simple rectangular blocks, for example triclinic or truncated-octahedral boxes. (UNVERIFIED)

An identifier that encodes the structure of a molecule as a short line of text, using the SMILES notation (Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System). It lets a small molecule be written, searched, and shared as plain text, and complements the InChI code. (UNVERIFIED)

A software development and management tool that translates a program's source code into a runnable program. Which compiler was used can affect a simulation's speed and, occasionally, its numerical results. (UNVERIFIED)

A plan specification that defines a named group of atoms selected from the system, so the group can be referred to by name during setup or analysis. It is the concept behind a Gromacs index (.ndx) file, where groups such as Protein or Water are listed. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular dynamics method in which the forces between atoms come from a classical (empirical) force field rather than from quantum-mechanical calculations. It is the most common and computationally affordable form of molecular dynamics. (UNVERIFIED)

An information content entity recording how the atoms and residues of a simulated system correspond to those of the experimental structure it was built from. The 2 rarely match: residues are renumbered, missing loops are built in, and hydrogens are added. Without this record, a simulation result cannot be related back to the numbering used in the literature. (UNVERIFIED)
A structural property that describes how many copies of a protein chain join together to form a working unit. Many proteins function only when several copies assemble into one complex. (UNVERIFIED)

An oligomeric state in which the protein works on its own as a single chain, not joined to copies of itself. A protein simulated as a single chain when it is really a pair will behave wrongly, because the surface that should be buried against its partner is exposed to water instead. The state is usually known from the experimental structure or from measurements in solution. (UNVERIFIED)

An oligomeric state in which 2 copies of a protein chain join together to form the working unit. The 2 copies bury a surface against each other that would otherwise face the solvent, so simulating only one gives a different answer. Many enzymes and most transcription factors work this way. (UNVERIFIED)

An oligomeric state in which 3 copies of a protein chain join together to form the working unit. Such an assembly usually has 3-fold symmetry, so its subunits are equivalent and the whole can be built from one. Viral coat proteins and several membrane channels take this form. (UNVERIFIED)

An oligomeric state in which 4 copies of a protein chain join together to form the working unit. The 4 may be 4 copies of one chain or 2 copies each of 2 different ones, which is the arrangement haemoglobin takes. Cooperative behaviour, where binding at one subunit changes the others, requires an assembly of this kind. (UNVERIFIED)

An oligomeric state in which 5 or more copies of a protein chain join together to form the working unit. Assemblies this large are usually symmetric rings or shells, so the whole is built by repeating one subunit. They are often too large to simulate atom by atom, which is where coarse-grained models are used instead. (UNVERIFIED)
A conformational state of a coronavirus spike protein describing how many of its receptor-binding domains are raised into the open position, ready to engage a host cell.

A system classification label naming the specific strain or sequence variant of the organism that the simulated molecule comes from, for example a particular variant of the COVID-19 virus. It groups simulations by biological origin.
A system classification label naming a non-standard version of a histone protein present in the structure (for example H2A.Z). Different histone versions can change how DNA is packaged and read.

A nucleic acid analysis tool that characterises RNA and DNA secondary structure and higher-order motifs directly from three-dimensional coordinates. Built on the x3DNA suite, it annotates base pairs, helices, stems, hairpin loops and multi-branch junctions, and produces schematic representations of the result. It is widely used for RNA structural bioinformatics and is integrated into viewers such as Jmol and PyMOL.

synonyms.val: Dissecting the Spatial Structure of RNA

definition.val: An information content entity that records which atoms of a molecular system a tool should act on. It may be a stored list of atom indices or an expression that is evaluated to produce that list. It says what to operate on, not what to do with it. (UNVERIFIED)

OBSOLETE. An information content entity that records the conditions and factors used when choosing which items to include in a study, such as which ligands to simulate. It states what was considered rather than what was chosen.

comments: Retired 2026-08-13, the day after it was minted. It was created to group three children of the retired MOLSIM:000310 plan specification, but only one of the three belonged: MOLSIM:002163 atom selection mask and MOLSIM:002233 atom index group went to MOLSIM:002251 atom selection specification instead, and MOLSIM:001035 validated ligand selection criteria turned out to be an object property that never belonged in a class tree. That left one child, MOLSIM:000143 ligand pairs selection criteria, which is itself the group its twelve criteria belong to. A search of the whole ontology found no other term that could join: every other label mentioning selection or criteria is a convergence threshold, an algorithm or an analysis, all correctly placed elsewhere. MOLSIM:000143 was re-parented to IAO:0000030 information content entity, where it sat before. Never present in a release file.

definition.val: A state that a molecule or molecular system occupies, characterised by its shape, its surroundings, its position on the energy surface, or its electronic configuration. It describes a condition the system is in, rather than a relationship to another molecule or a choice made when the system was built. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular termini state in which the N-terminus of a polymer chain is closed off with an acetyl group, so that the end carries no electric charge. Capping this way makes a short peptide behave more like a piece cut from the middle of a longer chain. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular termini state in which the C-terminus of a polymer chain is closed off with an N-methylamide group, so that the end carries no electric charge. It is the usual partner to an acetyl group at the other end of the chain. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular termini state in which the C-terminus of a polymer chain is closed off with a plain amide group, so that the end carries no electric charge. It is a smaller alternative to an N-methylamide cap. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular termini state in which the N-terminus of a polymer chain is left uncapped and carries a positive charge, as a free amine group does at the pH of most simulations. This is the usual choice when the chain being simulated is a whole protein rather than a fragment of one. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular termini state in which the C-terminus of a polymer chain is left uncapped and carries a negative charge, as a free carboxylic acid group does at the pH of most simulations. This is the usual choice when the chain being simulated is a whole protein rather than a fragment of one. (UNVERIFIED)

A non-bonded interaction parameter that specifies the distance beyond which van der Waals interactions are no longer calculated. Several programs set this separately from the electrostatic cut-off so that the two can take different values. (UNVERIFIED)

basicPropertyValues.val: AMBER 26 Reference Manual, p. 499, entry vdw_cutoff. States that es_cutoff and vdw_cutoff control the cutoffs for vdw and electrostatic direct force interactions separately, that cut must not be given as well, and that vdw_cutoff must be greater than or equal to es_cutoff.
GROMACS 2026.3 Reference Manual, p. 53, entry rvdw, which gives the distance for the LJ or Buckingham cut-off.

definition.val: A publication that surveys and summarises existing published work on a topic rather than reporting new primary results.
A publication that forms one titled part of an edited book, usually written by different authors from the other parts.

A document presenting the research carried out for an academic degree, submitted to and examined by the awarding institution. Simulation results are often reported here before they appear in any journal.
A publication that is one of the collected contributions to a scientific meeting.

An information content entity that records one property of a data source, such as how its data was produced or who may see it. These are deliberately kept apart from the data source hierarchy itself, which sorts sources only by what kind of resource they are, so that a single source can carry several descriptors at once.
A data source descriptor that records how the data held by a source was produced.
A data origin recording that the data was obtained by measurement in a laboratory rather than by calculation.
A data origin recording that the data was produced by calculation or simulation rather than by laboratory measurement.
A data source descriptor that records who may obtain the data held by a source.
A data access descriptor recording that the data may be obtained by anyone without permission or licence.
A data access descriptor recording that the data may be obtained only under some condition, such as an institutional membership, a licence, an embargo period, or a direct request to its holder.

An Extended PDB ID is the unique twelve-character code composed of a 'pdb_' header followed by 8 alphanumeric characters. Every Extended PDB ID is assigned to a experimentally determined biomolecular structure deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). This identifier serves to reference and retrieve PDB data. This format is the successor of the legacy four-character PDB ID.

An InChIKey is a fixed-length, 27-character alphanumeric hash derived from the InChI (International Chemical Identifier) code of a chemical structure, used to uniquely and compactly identify chemical compounds in databases and web searches.
An SI unit of time equal to 10^-15 seconds or one quadrillionth of a second. (UNVERIFIED)
A unit of pressure defined as 101,325 pascals (Pa) or 1.01325 bar, approximately equal to the average atmospheric pressure at sea level on Earth. (UNVERIFIED)

A unit of velocity, representing one angstrom (10^-10 meters) of distance traveled per nanosecond (10^-9 seconds) of time. It is commonly used in molecular dynamics simulations and studies of atomic-scale processes. (UNVERIFIED)

A unit of energy per amount of substance, defined as one kilocalorie of energy (1000 thermochemical gram calories) per one mole of substance. It is commonly used in chemistry and biology for thermodynamic quantities. (UNVERIFIED)

nodes.lbl: kilocalorie per mole per square angstrom

definition.val: A unit of energy per amount of substance per area, commonly used in molecular dynamics simulations for expressing force constants and restraint weights. (UNVERIFIED)
A unit of electric charge defined as the charge carried by a single proton. It is a fundamental physical constant, with a value of exactly 1.602176634 × 10^-19 coulombs. (UNVERIFIED)
A unit that measures a fluid's resistance to flow under the influence of gravity. It is the ratio of the fluid's dynamic viscosity to its density. (UNVERIFIED)

A centimeter-gram-second (CGS) unit of kinematic viscosity, defined as the kinematic viscosity of a fluid that passes one square centimeter in one second. It is equivalent to the unit Stokes (St). (UNVERIFIED)
A unit that measures the separation of positive and negative electrical charges within a system, indicating the system's overall polarity. (UNVERIFIED)
A centimeter-gram-second (CGS) unit of electric dipole moment, defined as 10^-18 statcoulomb-centimeters. One Debye is approximately equal to 3.33564 × 10^-30 coulomb-meters. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that finds the rotation bringing 2 matched sets of points into the closest possible agreement, by decomposing the matrix of their cross-correlations. It gives the rotation only, so the 2 sets must already have been centred on their averages. It is the standard way structures are superposed before any difference between them is measured. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that assigns secondary structure to each residue of a protein from its atomic coordinates. It combines hydrogen bond energies with backbone angle preferences, where the older DSSP method uses hydrogen bonds alone. The extra criterion makes its assignments agree more closely with those a crystallographer would make by eye. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical algorithm that describes a distribution as a weighted sum of several bell-shaped components, fitting the position, width and weight of each. It suits data made of several overlapping groups, where one component would fit none of them. Each component can then be treated as a conformational state. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical algorithm that fits a chosen family of distributions to data by finding the parameter values that make the data most likely, or most probable given a prior. Assuming a family lets a whole distribution be summarised by 2 or 3 numbers. The assumption is also the weakness: if the data do not follow that family, the fit is confidently wrong. (UNVERIFIED)

A statistical algorithm that estimates a distribution by fitting smooth polynomial pieces joined at chosen points, rather than assuming a named family. It can follow a shape that no standard distribution matches. Its accuracy depends on how many joining points are used, which must be chosen to avoid following noise. (UNVERIFIED)

An algorithm that computes the surface area of a molecule reachable by solvent, by placing test points over each atom's surface and counting those not buried by neighbouring atoms. The test points approximate rolling a solvent-sized sphere over the molecule. Its accuracy depends on how many test points are used, which is the one setting it has. (UNVERIFIED)

A similarity score giving how far the chemical features of 2 aligned molecules coincide, such as hydrogen bond donors, acceptors and charged groups. It complements a shape comparison, which cannot tell a hydrogen bond donor from an acceptor of the same size. "Color" here refers to feature type, not to any visual property. (UNVERIFIED)

A similarity score giving how far the volumes of 2 aligned molecules overlap, as the shared volume divided by the volume either occupies. It ranges from 0 for no overlap to 1 for identical shape. It considers only shape, so 2 chemically unlike molecules that fill the same space score highly. (UNVERIFIED)

A similarity score adding the shape score and the chemical feature score, giving a value between 0 and 2. Adding them weights shape and chemistry equally, which suits searching for a molecule that both fits a site and makes the same contacts. Reporting the 2 parts separately alongside it is usual, since the sum hides which one is high. (UNVERIFIED)

A molecular trajectory analysis format is a specialized file structure designed to store processed data derived from the analysis of a molecular dynamics simulation. These formats typically contain derived quantities, such as secondary structure timelines, pairwise distance matrices, or principal component vectors, rather than raw atomic coordinates. They allow for the efficient storage and rapid retrieval of complex analysis results without the need to re-process the massive original trajectory files.

A data format that stores spatial or statistical data describing how solvent molecules are distributed around a solute and what properties they carry there. Files in these formats usually hold a 3-dimensional grid of values such as local solvent density, charge distribution, or interaction energy. They are used to visualize hydration shells and to calculate thermodynamic properties of solvation. (UNVERIFIED)

A data format that stores the results of an electronic structure calculation, such as molecular orbitals, electron densities, basis sets or electrostatic potentials. Files in these formats are how quantum chemistry programs hand their results to visualization software and to other analysis tools. The group covers both program-specific formats and interchange formats. (UNVERIFIED)

A data source that holds data, observations or protocols recorded directly in a digital laboratory notebook system used by a research group. Unlike a public database or a formal publication, it contains raw internal records of day-to-day work and of the exact conditions of an experiment. Citing it says where the data came from when that data sits inside a system owned by one institution and has not yet been publicly deposited or peer reviewed.

A set of networked computers housed and administered within a single institution, used as one pooled resource. It differs from a national facility in being controlled locally, so access and software are decided by the group that runs it. Most routine simulation work is done on one of these rather than on a large shared machine. (UNVERIFIED)

A free energy analysis method that estimates the free energy of a single conformation by adding its internal potential energy to its solvation free energy. It leaves out the solute's internal entropy, on the assumption that this cancels when 2 similar states are compared. It is the reasoning that the end-point binding free energy methods rest on. (UNVERIFIED)

A computational method that predicts the structure of a complex between a protein and a short peptide. It is harder than docking a small rigid molecule, because a peptide has many rotatable bonds and usually has no fixed shape of its own until it binds. Methods for it therefore search over the peptide's conformation as well as its position. (UNVERIFIED)

Membrane placement analysis is a computational method used to determine the optimal position and orientation of a protein structure within a lipid bilayer. It calculates the most energetically favorable alignment by assessing the hydrophobicity of the protein surface and matching it to the hydrophobic core and polar interfaces of the membrane. This analysis is a critical prerequisite for setting up stable membrane protein simulations and for understanding how proteins anchor themselves in the cell membrane.

A validation method that checks an assembled molecular system for chemical and topological errors before a simulation is set up. It reports missing force field parameters, a non-integer net charge, and atoms placed on top of one another. It is run as the last step of system preparation, because each of those faults makes the resulting topology unusable. (UNVERIFIED)

The standard error of the mean (SEM) is data item denoting the standard deviation of the sample-mean's estimate of a population mean.

definition.val: The correlation coefficient of two variables in a data sample is their covariance divided by the product of their individual standard deviations. It is a normalized measurement of how the two are linearly related.

Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is a correlation coefficient which is a nonparametric measure of statistical dependence between two ranked variables. It assesses how well the relationship between two variables can be described using a monotonic function. If there are no repeated data values, a perfect Spearman correlation of +1 or −1 occurs when each of the variables is a perfect monotone function of the other.
Spearman's coefficient may be used when the conditions for computing Pearson's correlation are not met (e.g linearity, normality of the 2 continuous variables) but may require a ranking transformation of the variables

The standard deviation of a random variable, statistical population, data set, or probability distribution is a measure of variation which correspond to the average distance from the mean of the data set to any given point of that dataset. It also corresponds to the square root of its variance.

The Pearson's correlation coefficient is a correlation coefficient which evaluates two continuous variables for association strength in a data sample. It assumes that both variables are normally distributed and linearity exists. 
The coefficient is calculated by dividing their covariance with the product of their individual standard deviations. It is a normalized measurement of how the two are linearly related.

The coefficient of determination is a data item measuring the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable(s).
In the case of a linear regression mode, the coefficient of determination r2 is the quotient of the variances of the fitted values and observed values of the dependent variable.

definition.val: A hypothesis testing measure that represents the probability of obtaining a result at least as far from the value actually obtained as the value expected, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

basicPropertyValues.val:
Within the frequentist framework, a p-value is typically a p-value for two-sided test and the criterion for rejecting the null hypothesis is typically expressed as a p-value that is less than an alpha setting divided by 2. In some cases, the p-value is a p-value for one-sided test, and the criterion for rejecting the null hypothesis is typically expressed as a p-value that is less than an alpha setting. A p-value is preferably coded more precisely as a p-value for two-sided test or a p-value for one-sided test rather than using the code for p-value without specification. The code for p-value (without specification) may be used in contexts where the p-value reported is ambiguous.

Within the Bayesian framework, use the posterior predictive p-value.

a core relation that holds between a whole and its part

basicPropertyValues.val: Everything has itself as a part. Any part of any part of a thing is itself part of that thing. Two distinct things cannot have each other as a part.

Occurrents are not subject to change and so parthood between occurrents holds for all the times that the part exists. Many continuants are subject to change, so parthood between continuants will only hold at certain times, but this is difficult to specify in OWL. See http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/ro/docs/temporal-semantics/

Parthood requires the part and the whole to have compatible classes: only an occurrent have an occurrent as part; only a process can have a process as part; only a continuant can have a continuant as part; only an independent continuant can have an independent continuant as part; only a specifically dependent continuant can have a specifically dependent continuant as part; only a generically dependent continuant can have a generically dependent continuant as part. (This list is not exhaustive.)

A continuant cannot have an occurrent as part: use 'participates in'. An occurrent cannot have a continuant as part: use 'has participant'. An immaterial entity cannot have a material entity as part: use 'location of'. An independent continuant cannot have a specifically dependent continuant as part: use 'bearer of'. A specifically dependent continuant cannot have an independent continuant as part: use 'inheres in'.

definition.val: x precedes y if and only if the time point at which x ends is before or equivalent to the time point at which y starts. Formally: x precedes y iff ω(x) <= α(y), where α is a function that maps a process to a start point, and ω is a function that maps a process to an end point.

definition.val: A relation that links a molecular simulation system to the geometric shape of the simulation cell used to apply periodic boundary conditions. Those conditions mimic an infinite system by making a particle that leaves one side re-enter from the opposite side. Common shapes are cubic, triclinic and rhombic dodecahedron, and the choice affects both computational cost and how isotropic the system is. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a computational process or analysis step to the utility program from a molecular dynamics software suite that was used to perform it. For example, a trajectory analysis may use a particular trajectory processing utility, or system preparation a particular solvation tool. It records the exact tool used within a larger workflow, where that tool is one component of a bigger software package. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a structural alignment procedure or analysis step to the software program used to perform the alignment. Structural alignment superimposes molecular structures such as proteins or nucleic acids, so that their conformations can be compared or conserved regions found. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular structure to the origin from which its three-dimensional coordinates were obtained. The origin may be an entry in an experimental database such as the Protein Data Bank, the output of a computational prediction method such as homology modelling, or another defined source. Recording it lets a reader trace where a structure came from and judge its quality. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular simulation system to the overall physical context or medium it represents, such as an aqueous solution, a lipid bilayer, a vacuum or a crystal lattice. That context shapes the choice of simulation parameters, including boundary conditions and dielectric treatment, and how the results should be read.

A relation that links a molecular simulation system to the initial three-dimensional structural model of the molecular complex used as its starting point. That structure is often taken from experimental data such as a PDB entry, or from earlier computational modelling such as a docking pose. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a plan specification to the rules, checks or conditions applied to confirm that the chosen ligands, and the alchemical transformations between them, are suitable for a relative binding free energy calculation. Those checks may cover structural similarity, consistency of charge and protonation state, or avoiding transformations that inappropriately break or form covalent bonds. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links an enhanced sampling process to the geometric or collective variable along which the system is steered or biased, for example in steered molecular dynamics or umbrella sampling. Examples are the distance between two groups of atoms, an angle, a dihedral angle, or a more complex function of atomic coordinates.

A relation that links a molecular dynamics process to one of the discrete stages that make it up. The stages belong to the run rather than to the protocol, because one protocol may be followed by many runs. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular dynamics process to a schedule defining how one of its parameters varies over simulated time or integration steps. A parameter that changes during a run, such as a temperature being raised or a restraint being released, is not described by a single value. Without the schedule the record of the run would say only where it started. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a simulation stage to a continuity check assessing its temporal join with an adjacent stage. A long simulation is usually run as a chain of shorter stages, and a gap or an overlap between 2 of them makes the combined trajectory wrong. The check is what establishes that the stages really do join end to end. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a simulation stage to an error encountered while loading or parsing one of its data files. Recording the error keeps a failed or partial read visible instead of silently producing incomplete metadata. A record with an error attached should not be treated as equivalent to one without. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular simulation system to a high-level classification label describing its composition. It lets systems be grouped and searched by what they contain rather than by their file names. The labels are coarse on purpose, so that a whole collection can be sorted without reading each entry. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a data format to the specific convention or schema variant that a file follows. One named format often covers several incompatible layouts, so naming the format alone does not say how to read a file. The convention is what a reader has to match. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular dynamics process to the atom selection mask defining which atoms are subject to restraints. The mask is what turns "restrain the protein" into a definite set of atoms. A mask that selects the wrong atoms produces a simulation that runs normally and means something else. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular dynamics process to a simulation parameter that governs how it is carried out, such as the integration timestep, the non-bonded cutoff, or an output write interval. These settings are part of what a result means, not incidental detail. A simulation cannot be repeated or judged without them. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular dynamics process to the simulation protocol it was carried out according to. The protocol is the reusable plan and the process is one execution of it, so a single protocol may be followed by many runs. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular simulation system to the water model used to represent its solvent, such as TIP3P or SPC/E. The choice fixes the geometry and the charges of every water molecule, and it affects properties that depend on the solvent, including diffusion and the strength of hydrogen bonds. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that links a molecular simulation system to the chemical state chosen for the ends of its polymer chains, whether each end was closed off with a capping group or left uncapped and carrying a charge. The choice changes the total charge of the system, and it matters most for short peptides, where the two ends are a large part of the whole molecule. (UNVERIFIED)

A relation that groups properties quantifying the chemical composition of a molecular system, such as the total number of atoms, residues and molecules of each type. Those counts give the stoichiometry and the overall size of the system being simulated. (UNVERIFIED)
